vice-president of the commission. (es) mr president, we were just talking about aviation safety. now let's talk about maritime safety. ladies and gentlemen, this package we are discussing today is the penultimate stage and it is, of course, the completion of the work done over the last four years. i would remind you that in december 1999 we were faced with the problem of the sinking of the erika, a tragedy that all of you are aware of; then there was the sinking of the prestige. these two accidents have made citizens in different european countries look to europe and demand answers. we have taken many very important steps, and i think we can say without fear of being wrong that during this parliamentary term there has been a revolution in maritime safety within the european union and a dramatic improvement in the safeguards to protect our coasts and our citizens. today europe can say that it has a system at least equivalent to that of the countries in the world that are best able to protect themselves, and now there is no country in the world - contrary to what was happening four and a half years ago - that has more demanding measures. the risks and the seas are different, but at last we have a really ambitious and adequate system. we must move on and today we are going to discuss a fundamental element of the mechanism for combating and preventing pollution from ships, namely the system of criminal sanctions for pollution offences for which a part of a directive sets the framework, and then there is the instrument in the criminal field. in march 2003, the commission presented its proposal for a directive on pollution from ships and the introduction of penalties, including criminal penalties, for pollution offences. the commission proposes to introduce into community law the concept of illegal dumping of pollutants at sea. the proposal seeks to incorporate into our legal system the provisions of the international convention for the prevention of pollution from ships, the marpol convention. secondly, to ensure that those responsible for illegal dumping - not only the masters and shipowners, but also the shipowners and classification societies which may in some cases be involved in this type of liability - can be sued and are also subject to criminal sanctions under certain conditions. and thirdly, to define precisely the conditions under which responsibility can be demanded of each of those involved; in the commission's view, criminal liability can be demanded when the discharges are intentional and also, in the case of an accident, if the discharge is due to gross negligence. that is, intent and gross negligence. as you know, the commission also put forward a proposal for a framework decision on pollution from ships in may last year. this second proposal complements the proposal for a directive and essentially regulates aspects of the criminal field, namely the harmonization of penalties and questions of judicial cooperation in criminal matters. the principle of criminal liability and the imposition of the corresponding penalty must be established in law and, in the commission's view, by means of a directive, which, in the present state of the treaties, is the only really effective instrument for sanctions to be able to be incorporated into the law of all the member states and therefore to be effective deterrents. the three objectives i have mentioned are clear, feasible and, for us, inescapable. however, for some member states, the proposal for a directive currently on the table goes too far: its objectives seem too ambitious. the council has not yet defined its position on this, but i have been able to verify the doubts of most of the ministers, who do not seem convinced that we should continue along this path. some have a clear intention of looking very much down on the ambitions contained in the commission's proposal for a directive. i must confess that i am deeply disappointed with the outcome of the council's work. work is proceeding very slowly and the delay has not allowed us to respond to the expectations of our fellow citizens or to the demands made by the heads of state and government who had called for the parliament and the council to adopt this directive by the end of 2003. i am convinced that i can count, once again, on the support of this house. the position adopted by parliament will be decisive and will help to unblock the situation. the third issue is the transfer of vessels between registers in the european union. in addition to the aspects of penalties - the treatment or punishment with penalties of certain actions in the field of pollution of the seas and the production of discharges - we will discuss the transfer of cargo and passenger vessels between community registers. twelve years after the adoption of the current regulation, it is urgent - in the light of experience gained and in the context of the imminent enlargement of the community fleet - to update the oldest text of our maritime safety acquis. under the current regulation, only cargo vessels may benefit from the scheme under certain conditions. the first objective of the commission's proposal is that passenger ships should also be able to benefit from a rapid transfer between registers in community countries, which is less burdensome for our operators and therefore facilitates the operation of the sector and makes it more competitive. this will of course be done while maintaining the high level of maritime safety resulting from respect for the relevant international conventions. in addition to this objective, the proposal aims to improve the flow of information between the maritime administrations of the union states and to better align the regime applicable to transfers between registers with the community acquis, especially with the port state control and classification society directives that we have adopted in the erika packages. the council's discussions have shown that there is a consensus on the need to strengthen the current regime for the exchange of registration. the amendments contained in the text of the council's general guidelines of 5 december 2003 help to define the scope of the regulation and, to better articulate it, with the detention and denial of access procedures of the port state control directive. the commission fully supports these views. mr president, with these two packages of measures we are taking a final step in improving and strengthening maritime safety at the level of the european union, an area where, throughout this legislature, i believe we have made remarkable progress. i would like to thank parliament once again for its systematic support and backing of the measures we have been proposing and also for its cooperation and its contribution of positive proposals throughout this period.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of ships is not compromised. i feel it is my duty - or rather my right - to criticize you when appropriate, and at the same time to praise you when appropriate. and as far as maritime safety is concerned, i think the commission has done its job, in the name of the general european interest. this report, if not the most important of all the reports, is nevertheless to be credited with all the achievements of the last four years. however, the task is not finished, and it is enough to read the sterckx report to realise how much a new legislature is needed to complete the system. in any case, the starting point is simple: every boat has a flag that belongs to a country, since there is no european flag. an attempt to do so was made 15 years ago, but it was never successful. the first text on the change of register dates back more than ten years. the commission proposal and the accompanying parliament report are designed to adapt to the new situation, as a lot of water has flowed under the bridge since then. this report, like the commission's text, is based on three main lines. first, it includes passenger ships. these had not been included in the first directive for a reason given at the time, namely that the regulations differed greatly from one member state to another. that is why our committee and parliament did not include passenger ships in the text at the time. but since then many important decisions have been taken - i am thinking in particular of the solas convention - many improvements have been made, the regulations have been approximated on many points, so that it now seems normal to include passenger ships in the regulation. the second part of the report is rather similar in its argumentation, since it is concerned with coordinating community instruments in the field of maritime safety, in short, with integrating all the legislation that has been adopted over time, and in particular the erika i and erika ii packages. finally, the third axis aims to strengthen cooperation between national maritime administrations. these are the three main lines of my report, which of course correspond to those of the commission's proposal. the importance of these reforms is also due to the fact that europe will grow and expand to ten new states. i would remind our colleagues that we are going to welcome, of course, ten states, but above all two island states with a very large fleet, malta and cyprus, and it seems appropriate to complete this regulation before 1 may 2004. that is why we should adopt the text after a single reading in parliament, as we did at the time for the simple hulls, so as not to waste time and to make maritime safety the objective, rather than fighting over purely procedural matters, the idea being to find the most intelligent or at least the least stupid compromise possible. the council has tabled several amendments, and your rapporteur proposes that you accept them, since they do not change the substance of the text. some of them deal with technical changes, for example by specifying the ships to which the regulation does not apply, in particular warships. some amendments also specify that states may enforce rules which are different from those of the solas convention, provided that they are no less stringent, and other amendments impose on each state the obligation to submit an annual report and insist on the former to facilitate the implementation of the regulation. the most important request comes from the commission, since it insists that a vessel which has been detained more than once as a result of an inspection in a port, during the three years preceding the request for a change of register, will not be able to benefit from a simplified regime, unlike other vessels. in short, it is a precaution for vessels which have revealed a number of weaknesses during checks. an amendment has been tabled by one of our colleagues to put the starry flag on the flag which changes register. i find this amendment sympathetic and symbolic, and our committee voted in favour of it, but the council does not wish to accept this amendment, because it would only concern ships changing registers and not the whole fleet. i am willing to give it up, but i hope that one day we will put the star-spangled banner on the flag of our ships so that, although the national flag is there, the little corner of europe can also sail the seas of the world. that, ladies and gentlemen, is the very meaning of this report, and i hope you will support it.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, our vote on this report is eagerly awaited. the violence and passion of the political debate on this subject, i have experienced throughout this year of work. before maastricht, the choice of public authorities, local and national, coexisted without difficulty with the common market. with the single market, conflicts and concerns are heightened. the solution to these problems is still literally blocked by taboos. some say that the record of liberalization is excellent. on the other hand, some consider public service and competition to be incompatible. others, and i hope there will be many of us, believe that liberalisation has produced both positive and negative effects, that a better balance between market and non-market principles in the substance of the rules is needed, and that it would improve cohesion and efficiency. a fair assessment of reality is necessary, because the certainty that the market does everything better becomes a dogmatic truth and divides europe into two camps. the commitment of the legislator to restore balance, to reconcile the conflicting principles in the great tradition of european civilization, seems to me indispensable. many colleagues accept the idea of a balance, but consider that only local, regional and national public authorities have the power to decide this. i fully agree with the idea of defending and strengthening the freedom of decentralised administration, but i am convinced that the market will reduce it even more if the union does not also take up its share of guarantees and co-responsibility. and our community will only make sense if it also offers complementary public goods, for example in education, railways or information. my colleagues have rejected this view. i stand by my view that subsidiarity and co-responsibility go together. throughout history, europeans, whether christian or humanist, liberal or socialist, have considered the organisation of the commons to be essential to the development of the individual and life in society. let's not be in there. let us work hard to bridge the ethical gaps between our national communities on public goods. in the immediate future, why a framework directive? not for the pleasure of legislating, because we abuse it. but now it's necessary. it is time for the legislator to interpret the treaties himself instead of leaving all powers to the commission: legislative, executive, judicial, self-assessment. the convention allows this, inserting a new article to this effect in the draft constitutional treaty, and the realities demand it. first, a legal framework must give a positive - and no longer merely derogating - status to services of general interest, a status which the market and competition rules will then be bound to respect. secondly, the serious uncertainty surrounding the distinction between services of economic and non-economic interest must be overcome. essential areas such as education, health and water must not be liberalised and the increasingly mixed situations where social, economic and ecological are interwoven must be addressed. to this end, my proposals aim to give municipalities, non-profit or mixed-economy enterprises and public-private partnerships a general framework of increased guarantees for their deployment. thirdly, the principles of funding and organisation need to be clarified. the altmark judgment on state aid is positive, but it contains serious uncertainties in the calculation of costs, and care must be taken not to criminalise public operators. fourthly, we want a pluralistic and independent evaluation method to be established. to refuse it would be to deny democracy. i would add that there is, of course, compatibility between a framework directive and sectoral directives. we therefore ask the commission to follow up quickly on the consultation it has launched and on the vote of this parliament by answering: what commitments on the legal framework, funding or evaluation? and we reject the continuation of the altmark judgment by means of article 86 (3), that is to say, without codecision. i would like to thank very much the many associations, ngos, trade unions, networks of municipalities and the companies consulted, whose opinions have informed and supported me. like elected representatives, they legitimately want to have a much greater say in eu policies and rules. i would also like to thank my colleagues on the committee on economic and monetary affairs, who have put a lot of effort into this, and especially those who have sought compromises. unfortunately, a majority said no to a framework directive, no to a democratic evaluation. in doing so, it has not only rejected my proposals and our compromises. it simply abandoned the resolution of this parliament, which was voted in 2001. tomorrow you can reinstate your commitment. i am convinced, ladies and gentlemen, that many of you, on the right and on the left, are committed to defending and promoting services of general interest. i therefore urge you not to adopt a bloc approach - partisan or national - and to decide amendment by amendment, article by article, in the general interest of europeans. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. mr president, let us simply remember that today's debate on the future of services of general interest does not take place at any moment in the history of europe, since europe is currently in the midst of a debate on its future, on its constitution, and we are preparing to welcome many citizens from eastern countries. i am mentioning this because it seems to me that there is a parallel between, on the one hand, the difficulties we experienced in the debate on the draft constitution in reaching agreement and in having a european law and recognition of positive law for services of general interest enshrined, and, on the other hand, the obstacles, not the least of which, we have encountered, or at least the obstacles which the excellent rapporteur, mr herzog, had to face in the economic and monetary affairs committee, in order to put this idea forward. i also believe that it would be extremely damaging if this report were less ambitious than the compromise - mr president, first of all i should like to say how far, despite the enormous work of philippe herzog, the report from the economic and monetary affairs committee is from the expectations and hopes of an offensive european regulation on the question of services of general interest. my group cannot accept that. the text has become an ode to liberalisation, with the intention of making the competition law the sole regulator. for example, recital h argues that liberalisation of important sectors of the internal market is a factor of technological progress and economic efficiency, and paragraph 13 welcomes liberalisation in the areas of telecommunications, postal services, transport and energy. even the moderate proposal in the langen report, which we have voted on here, calling on the commission to carry out a precise and comparative assessment of the real impact of liberalisation policy before taking further steps, is not supported by this report. the report also dismisses, under false pretexts, the objective of a framework directive to define more precisely services of general interest and the obligations arising therefrom for states and public or private operators. only the basic education and social protection systems would remain in the public domain. we are a long way from an approach that is essential in terms of fundamental rights: rights to energy, water, transport, housing, communication and information. however, the general interest services should be tasked with ensuring these rights for citizens through a number of principles: equal access for all, information, consultation, participation of users and employees, financial sustainability. this ambition is impossible with the sole objective of pursuing the liberalization we have started without any compromise. this text, as it stands, is unacceptable. the expectations and hopes born of the green paper are key public services for the implementation of economic, social and environmental rights; it is a europe which really aspires to meet the needs of the greatest number of people, in solidarity. on the basis of these remarks, my group will support all amendments which seek to remove the constant references to liberalisation and those which strengthen the concept of services of general interest worthy of the name. my group reiterates the need for evaluation. it recalls that services of general interest concern services of prime importance to citizens. it also expressed its willingness to confirm unambiguously the right of territorial authorities to retain their freedom of choice in the way in which they manage the services of general interest for which they are responsible. this is the minimum to make services of general interest a driving force for a europe of solidarity.
mr president, some people are playing with fire when they think they are putting an end to the abuses of community competition law. such deviations would require a change in the law or, at the very least, an explicit and unreserved exemption for the public service. the objective must remain the quality of equal service for all and not a criterion of profitability which leads to competition. it is therefore dangerous to try to define the general interest service missions at european level. firstly, they will no longer be consistent with the diversity of territories and national practices, and secondly, there is no will on this point and no majority, even a simple one, can be found. my group is in favour of a reflection to identify themes of general interest for users at european level, by ensuring funding capacity. we are a long way from that green paper and that report, which welcome the successes achieved so far with liberalisation. the draft constitution of the convention rejected by the brussels european council would have changed nothing, services of general interest would have remained subject to competition law. the objectives of the construction are clear: it is to dismantle existing public services in some member states. for my group, it is important to be able to discuss this democratically with our peoples, recognising in the end their right to choose the model they wish to see developed in the future to ensure cohesion between citizens and between territories. in conclusion, we will not support this text, although we will of course support the less bad proposals here and there. we are thus responding to the rapporteur's call, but we are inviting him to further question the merits of adopting the overall text.

in writing. - (fr) i voted in favour of the pex report, which is a major step forward in the fight to improve safety at sea. need i say that more than 6 million tonnes of polluting waste are deliberately dumped into the sea every year? it is imperative that we fight these sea-weeds, who consider the sea to be a dumping ground! the polluters must be punished severely and all parties involved in the transport of goods must be held accountable. prevention is better than cure. the fight against these unscrupulous people must therefore be more effective and more realistic. in fact, the number of people caught red-handed is minimal compared to the actual number of intentional polluting acts. furthermore, the procedure is often lengthy before these persons are convicted and given a comprehensive punishment, which is not always the case, so that they do not start again. i would first of all like to support cooperation between the port police authorities of the various coastal states. secondly, a common european coast guard could be set up, provided that its effectiveness is strictly controlled.
in writing. - (fr) we have supported the amendments aimed at strengthening maritime safety. we approve the extension of the scope of the regulation to passenger vessels, the coordination with the other community instruments and the strengthening of cooperation between national maritime authorities. at a time when the eu is expanding to include malta and cyprus, thus becoming the world's leading maritime power, these much-needed changes are urgently needed. the two island states must at all costs raise the morale of their flag, which is a veritable flag of convenience in the service of the 'sea wines'. but we must also condemn those who, like france, have introduced a 'b-flag'. french shipowners shall now use only the flag of the french southern and antarctic territories. in this way, they have employed up to 65% of seafarers of foreign nationality on their vessels registered in france (which allows them to receive, for example, substantial aid and subsidies). wages, working and living conditions are of course dependent on the seafarer's country of origin and are not proportionate to his qualifications. this exploitation allows for colossal profits at the expense of the dignity, rights, health and sometimes even the lives of the crews, who come mainly from the poorest countries on earth. this is the real scandal at the shipping register.
in writing. - (fr) in the vidal-quadras roca report on spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste and in the seppänen report on the safety of nuclear installations, we have supported all the amendments which sought to introduce greater safety in the operation of the installations as well as in the treatment and storage of radioactive waste. on the other hand, we have not supported the amendments which removed any timetable for when safety should be increased, sometimes for technical reasons, but the result is that the member states are allowed to do as they wish. without ignoring the fact that nuclear power is dangerous in itself, the fact that the heads of government cannot be trusted because they always put the economic interests of private corporations ahead of the human interests of the people is still the greatest danger.
(parliament adopted the legislative resolution) the spread of radioactive waste is a colossal problem for the environment and for public health. however, countries such as france are resuming their programme of nuclear power plant construction, which has the same shortcomings as the previous plants at this level. at the same time, the idea of liberalization carries with it both social and environmental dangers, for example by increasingly using subcontractors to maintain nuclear installations. in this connection, the amended vidal-quadras roca report, while claiming to contribute to better control of nuclear waste, contains serious shortcomings in two respects. it maintains the right of a member state to export its waste to a third country (although, to an improvement, it provides for 'prior written informed consent by states') and it promotes the deep-sea disposal of radioactive waste, which is strongly criticised by the surrounding populations and by a large number of scientists. that is why we voted against the report. the nuclear sector confirms that it is prohibitively expensive and enjoys scandalously favourable conditions compared with sectors producing 'clean' energy. we have to reverse this mindset. we therefore join the joint demonstration against nuclear power which will take place on saturday, 17 january, in paris.
the european parliament has already expressed its concern about the situation in the middle east, and it is therefore asking the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the situation in the middle east is not further aggravated by the threat of nuclear weapons. in fact, only nuclear energy - which has seen spectacular advances in research and which already provides us with an abundance of quality energy in complete safety - can meet the desire to preserve the environment, the demand for energy independence and the colossal challenge of the growth of the developing countries. is it really reasonable to believe that the energy demand derived from development can be met by renewable forms of energy in countries such as india or china? is it justified to condemn european nuclear energy to a definitive halt when it is the only one which can, through its experience and excellence in the field, really help to secure the new entities which in these third countries will not wait for the green light from the union to establish themselves? the energy problem, which is a sensitive subject for the european union and of vital importance to three quarters of the world's population, can only be solved by a dispassionate and pragmatic approach to the problem, which is far from the brain-stem and fantasies of environmental integrationism.
- mr president, among the many failures that marked the history of the european union in 2003 - the split over iraq, sweden's rejection of the euro, the collapse of the stability pact, the fiasco of the constitutional project - the defeat of the commission in cancun - we debated it here a short while ago - could have been regarded as a minor incident. the vast majority of countries and peoples welcomed the failure of the cancun conference. but the earth did not stop turning, nor did the world stop trading. we could have stayed where we are and therefore preserved our ways of life, because that is what it is all about, the greed of multinational markets. but that was without the commission's activism, without your activism, commissioner lamy, if i may say so. but this activism is not due to any economic or social necessity, and we have heard no complaints about the failure of cancun, but rather to your willingness to exercise and defend the commission's monopoly of representation and negotiation in the field of international trade and foreign trade. this real leap forward which you propose is in no way guided by the interests of europe, but by the interests of the brussels commission itself, at a time when the danger to our foreign trade, commissioners, is not the absence of new outlets for our products, but of course the insurmountable, unbearable handicap imposed on us by the autism of the european central bank, which gives us the most expensive currency in the world, and by no means the strongest.
in writing. - is the european commission deaf? this is the question that inevitably comes to mind when reading his guidelines for the relaunch of the wto's international trade negotiations in the doha round. in fact, it seemed clear to us in the aftermath of the cancun failure - we had said so in the european parliament's chamber - that the impasse in the negotiations showed the need to revise the objective of global free trade and to reintroduce the idea of a globalisation controlled by the peoples. the commission's programme recommends, in the words of the commission, 'a revision of the strategy to achieve the eu's objectives in the form of a refreshed negotiating position'. this self-contradictory sentence announces that there will be no in-depth revision, but simple adjustments in the margin. the commission maintains its priority objectives of free market access, free global competition and free investment (the so-called singapore issues), which are certainly interesting, but it should now give due weight to other concerns, in our interest as well as in that of the developing countries. it is now necessary to lay down the rules for international trade which better respects the sovereignty of peoples and is more compatible with the protection of the environment and public health.
in writing. - has the commission taken account of the cancun conference? the commission's communication, which was presented with a view to a possible relaunch of the negotiations on the development agenda launched in 2001, makes it difficult to say. his alleged "flexibility" on the singapore issues - grooming on the sidelines - his call for a "balance between rights and the market" and his desire to "ease up" on his positions in no way reflect the neoliberal european orientations. the commission's credits remain that it is scorned, that it is not self-critical and/or that it is not questioned. in the face of pascal lamy's assertions - endorsed by the council - the poorest countries are neither happy with the so-called new proposals nor satisfied with the policies implemented since seattle. on the contrary, the people of the south are organising themselves and taking a stand against the european and wto pretensions. the opening up of trade in services provided for by the gatt, the no less sacred opening up of the market - which is seen as an obvious benefit for the developing countries! - are dangers which the countries of the south have well identified. international relations, cooperation and exchanges on an equal footing, respectful of individual and collective fundamental rights deserve better. a public debate, supported by the elected representatives, to refute this logic is now essential.

- madam president, today, as every day, more than 8 000 people have died of aids because of lack of treatment. more than 4 million sick africans are in dire need of treatment and only 50,000 people have access to it. aids is not the only scourge afflicting the countries of the south: tuberculosis is spreading rapidly and kills 2 million people every year, malaria kills 1 to 2 million people every year and affects 300 to 500 million people. however, there are treatments available that can cure these diseases or significantly reduce mortality. but these treatments are expensive, too expensive, for countries that can only spend a paltry sum on their health systems, so that the drugs are for the north and the coffins are for the south. fortunately, things are starting to move. progress in 2003 was marked by some hopeful developments: the who initiative to provide treatment to 3 million patients by 2005, the agreement reached on 30 august 2003 in geneva by wto members, the decision by the south african government to launch a national treatment programme, the continued fall in the price of antiretroviral drugs on the world market and the eur 600 million european-developing countries' partnership clinical trials programme. these initiatives are very encouraging, but they are still far from sufficient. the union itself is slow to deliver on its financial promises and the sandbæk report is timely, it confirms the commitment of the european union and sets an ambition that is up to the challenge. it recalled that the highest priority must be access to medicines for all patients, in line with the doha declaration. the existence of patents should therefore not constitute a barrier to the production or purchase of life-saving medicines. the report also strongly emphasises that the prevention and treatment of communicable diseases is a matter for everyone, as they are a global public good. it sets an ambitious target for the financial commitment of the european union and its member states of €1 billion per year. by adopting this report, europe will reaffirm its intention to play an important role in the fight against these scourges.

- madam president, we will vote for this report because it describes the disaster of poverty-related diseases. for anyone who reads this report with a modicum of humanity and reason, the simple fact is a real indictment of our economic and social system, which tolerates the fact that millions of human beings die of curable diseases, including tuberculosis and malaria. the rest of the text is nothing but a statement of impotence. the impotence is not the fault of the rapporteur alone, but of the whole system. parliament is called upon to vote, but it does not have the power to touch the root of the problem. the only way to effectively combat poverty-related diseases is to combat poverty and, therefore, to combat the glaring inequalities of a social organisation where some individuals can appropriate and accumulate more wealth than whole countries. what does it mean, for example, to propose - and i quote - that the european pharmaceutical industry should be involved in the fight against poverty-related diseases? it is well known that pharmaceutical trusts seek to make a profit even at the expense of the poorest, and that there is no question of them distributing medicines, even if they are a hundred times more expensive, to patients who cannot afford them. furthermore, when these trusts have no hope of making a profit because the disease only affects poor countries, they stop research, as the report itself notes, citing sleeping sickness as an example. the pharmaceutical industry should operate under the control of society, without private profit, and produce the necessary medicines to distribute to all who need them. this would not yet end poverty, but it could contribute to some equality in care.
the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the new partnership for africa's development - nepad - is a political initiative which was adopted in october 2001 by five african heads of state: presidents mbeki of south africa, bouteflika of algeria, mubarak of egypt, obasanjo of nigeria and wade of senegal. these five countries now constitute the nepad steering committee. nepad is part of an ambitious project known as the 'renaissance of africa'. the partnership aims to enable africa to become master of its own destiny and is based on the desire to set an intra-african dynamic based on example. nepad member states are committed to respect for human rights, conflict prevention and resolution, the principles of democracy and good governance, but also, in a cultural revolution, to the fight against corruption. in short, this is african regional integration which would create the best conditions for encouraging private investors to participate in the economic and social development of these african countries. finally, a credible african initiative, which is based on the principle that the participation of the private sector is an indispensable complement to public aid, in the face of the immense needs of the african continent. the report is based on two main pillars: conflict prevention and resolution and good governance. peace and stability are the prerequisites for any development. this is true for public investment, but even more so for private investment. after a conflict, governments can resume investment fairly quickly. the same cannot be said for private investors, who must first regain confidence. in this context, the conflict in côte d'ivoire is likely to have negative consequences for the region's economy for many years to come. good governance is as essential as stability. democracy and respect for the rule of law are necessary conditions for economic and human development. with nepad, it is the africans themselves who ensure that these principles are respected and who make strong commitments. nepad has ten priority themes, the most important of which are: good public governance, good governance of the private economy, infrastructure - which is important - education and health, of course, agriculture, the environment, energy, and finally, difficult access to the markets of developed countries. nepad has received very favourable reactions in the industrialised countries, and particularly in the european union and the g8, as we saw last year in evian, even though the aid that has resulted has not always met the expectations of the initiating countries. overall, the commission's report welcomes the nepad initiative and calls for its prompt implementation. however, it does highlight areas for improvement and warns of potential dangers. the report takes note of the criticisms of many african civil society actors and encourages the african union member states, and in particular the donor countries, to allow the active and democratic participation of all segments of civil society: ngos, trade unions, employers' organisations, churches. the report also recalls that nepad is a socio-economic programme of the african union for the development of africa, and not an independent institution. it reiterated its conviction that all matters relating to the impetus and parliamentary control of nepad must of course be left to the pan-african parliaments which will be set up by the end of the year, while avoiding duplication of effort, double spending and institutional proliferation and overlap. finally, this report attaches the utmost importance to the implementation and democratic parliamentary scrutiny of the african peer review mechanism. in conclusion, this report is balanced. it represents the essence of the political sensibilities of this parliament. i would like to see it voted as it stands, without amendments, apart from a few oral amendments.

- madam president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i do not think i will be able to adopt the optimistic tone of the first speeches, and in particular of yours, madam commissioner, on cultural diversity, for several reasons. the first is that this international convention or instrument was a utopia until very recently. i remember that my group and i organised a public hearing in the autumn of 2002 to bring this idea to parliament. i think we have to be modest and i am not saying that this idea came from europe and the european union. it came from countries like canada, and from countries around the world that have banded together with some european countries. so i can only applaud the fact that this utopia is becoming a reality in the european union, but i think we must be modest. i am calling for modesty because i would like this future convention not to be just another declaration. we know the declarations for cultural diversity, we can make them, but now we have to draw up a binding and normative convention that allows us to settle disputes in a market context. i mean that cultural diversity also has to do with the question of the market. we must not hide the fact that combining cultural diversity and the market is a considerable challenge. that is why i am modest and not always optimistic in this respect. the third reason why i am not very optimistic is that i am not sure that we are an example to follow, as much as we like to say so. indeed, are we really in agreement within the european union to promote cultural diversity and, if so, what kind of diversity? - mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, the irish presidency is now given the heavy task of continuing the intergovernmental conference and of trying to bring together positions which differ not merely on technical points but also on conceptual grounds of sovereignty. you said earlier, mr president of the council, that the new constitution should meet the expectations of the citizens and enable the union to play a more coherent role in the world. if that were all there was to it, everyone would agree. but there is another crucial and much more difficult question: how can we cooperate in preserving democracy? should we seek to eliminate the independence of national sovereignty, in particular by majority voting, as the draft constitution states, or should we, on the contrary, preserve the sovereignty, and hence the national democracies, of the member states? we must make this clear to the citizens and to that end we urge the irish presidency to begin by taking a public and precise account of the points of agreement and disagreement in the igc. of course, this assessment would not prejudge the future, because we know that there is no agreement on anything as long as there is no agreement on everything, but it would at least make it possible to engage in a concrete debate and to inform citizens seriously. we also hope that governments will use the coming months to better assess the impact of the project. for example, the irish presidency's priorities, published by the 'sources of europe' website, show that you hoped - i said 'hope' - that accession negotiations with turkey could start at the end of 2004. could you tell us, therefore, what turkey's place would be in the institutions of the future constitution, which would be made to last - everyone tells us that every day? in writing. - (fr) the this report aims to protect the tuna fishing and processing industry in the eu from external competition. this objective is questionable, not least because we in the community already have the largest tuna fleet in the world and exploit fishery resources all over the globe, including in a number of poor countries. in addition, there is often competition from fishing fleets, which may be operating under the flags of other countries, but which belong to investors in the eu. the report expresses legitimate concern about the decline in tuna fishery resources. competition, which is a source of waste and crisis in all sectors of industry, has even more fatal consequences when it comes to natural resources, which can be completely used up if they are subject to unrestrained and irrational competition. the only logical conclusion to be drawn from this report is that a system based on competition is harmful and that collective, systematically planned management is the only sensible way of managing natural resources. management should be carried out at global level and not for the sole purpose of protecting eu production. the tuna have a boring tendency to disregard borders and territorial waters! we have abstained from the vote.
in writing. - (fr) the the eu tuna industry should be looking bright. it is a profession with enterprising operators, the quality is high, especially in france and spain, and it is a foodstuff which is healthy and natural, and the demand for it is high and growing. and yet the european union's competitiveness is weakened, which is the fault of the commission, despite the fact that it pretends to be the one and only true representative of the 'common good' in europe. the strict and ever-increasing requirements of community law, in particular those relating to safety, control, health conditions for production, environmental protection and social protection, mean that the costs of the eu fleet and processing undertakings are much higher than those of competitors. the commission is driven by an ideology which prescribes systematic and complete openness, which also applies to products from the sea. the list of countries benefiting from tariff preferences and from a particularly opaque system of certificates of origin is thus constantly being extended. in addition, the opening of a quota for tuna fillets and canned tuna for thailand, the philippines and indonesia is to be mentioned. the rapporteur points to 'the opening of the community market to foreign products, which are subject to fewer requirements and insufficient controls and which undermine the competitiveness of the community industry'. it is time to put an end to this discrimination which is being imposed by the commission to the detriment of our economies and employment.

- mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating our rapporteur on my own behalf for his work and the comprehensiveness of his proposals in the area of job-creating services. of course, we may be more or less in favour of some of these proposals. i would nevertheless like to see the whole package as an important contribution to this, at a time when unemployment is hitting many people hard and precarious jobs and contracts are proliferating. moreover, in order to make things clear, after these personal congratulations, i must say, as the spokesman for the gue/ngl group, our reservations in view of the constant reference to competition, the market and its rules, and also our disagreement with too strict application of the principle of mutual recognition in a sector which also covers public services and services of the social economy. it should also be borne in mind that we consider - and i shall be brief on this point today - that the deindustrialisation of europe is not inevitable, especially since in terms of jobs it is and will be increasingly difficult to compensate for the disappearance of industrial jobs by service jobs. that being said and recalled, it is very important, as you have done, madam rapporteur, to highlight the importance of this service sector, as it is important to highlight the potential and the conditions for job creation. it is even more necessary for us to say what the real needs are in terms of services. this is obvious in the case of care, in the case of children and babies, in the case of disabled people and the elderly. for these women, the service sector is a necessary condition for maintaining full citizenship, regardless of age, physical or health. but at this point i also want to make it clear that there is a need for a legal, legislative or conventional framework to avoid the detours that lead to the precariousness that exists in the american system. this is why existing service sector occupations need to be upgraded to provide quality jobs with good pay and working conditions. the quality of this new form of employment, parttime work in this case, needs to be improved by ensuring that the same high level of protection and job security is guaranteed to all workers and by improving working conditions for women. the gender pay gap and the gap in access to employment and promotion must be reduced. finally, cooperation in the fight against undeclared work must be strengthened. our rapporteur, the members of our committees have done a good job. and if, like the majority of my group, i believe that the implementation of these measures will not solve all the fundamental problems of employment and work, i am, mr president, personally in favour of any form of improvement, provided that the improvements are real.
commission. mr president, i shall explain some of the key points that may be of interest to members of parliament, in particular the amendments tabled by this parliament. i shall summarise my reply at the end of this debate in five points. firstly, some amendments call into question the current legislation and cannot therefore be accepted. this concerns particularly the limitation of the scope of application of the directive to liberal professions, the suppression of the recognition of formal qualifications for many crafts and trades professions, the limitation of recognition to qualifications at the same level and the several other more restrictive requirements for recognition. my second point concerns facilitation of cross-border service provision. a real simplification of temporary and occasional service provision implies less formalities. adequate guarantees to consumers can be provided through comprehensive information, and declarations to competent authorities and pro-forma registration can be accepted for healthcare professions. in any case, formal control of qualifications by host member states is not compatible with a real facilitation of cross-border service provision. thirdly, consolidation is not the appropriate framework for the introduction of new harmonising provisions; that requires in-depth consideration by all the interested parties and a specific impact assessment. fourthly, enlargement justifies a simpler organisation of recognition systems. community procedures have to be limited to union-wide measures and this fully justifies the new approach for recognition of medical and dental specialities common to only some member states, which will improve the likelihood of their continuing development. fifthly, enlargement also demands simpler management mechanisms, particularly through one single comitology committee. the commission is willing to contribute to this goal by setting up an expert group and by introducing more open and flexible consultation mechanisms with interested parties. the commission's opinion on the individual amendments of which there are many, as we all know has been provided in writing and will be distributed shortly. commission´s position on amendments by parliament: see annex. furthermore, i am confident that the valuable efforts made by the european parliament will provide a good basis for further constructive discussions. lastly, i should also like to congratulate mrs gebhardt on her birthday next week.

- mr president, the situation in haiti is catastrophic because of the violence of the armed gangs on which the regime relies, but even more so because of the immense poverty of the majority of its population. its leader aristide certainly does not deserve any sympathy, if only because he has betrayed the hopes his people had placed in him. but it is extremely disgusting when the political representatives of the great powers, especially france and the united states, who bear an overwhelming responsibility for the fate of haiti, pose as lecturers or moralists. indeed, if this country, which was two centuries ago one of the richest in the caribbean, has become one of the poorest in the world, it is because it has never ceased to be plundered and because france, the former colonial power, has never forgiven it for having won its independence by arms and thanks to the revolt of its slaves. for decades, haiti, which had become independent, suffered from a blockade by france, but with the complicity of the united states and britain, to force the country to pay compensation to the former owners of the chased slaves. it is certainly demagogy that aristide is now demanding the mr president, i would like to ask you about the information you gave to the european parliament on 12 january. you referred to the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the basis of rule 7 (4) of our rules of procedure, the letter which was sent to you concerning the mandate of mr michel raymond. in the present context, where the question of the status of members of the european parliament is putting the spotlight back on this house and its privileges, at a time when its committee on budgetary control is harassing the slightest fraud, the slightest embezzlement, the slightest indiscretion with regard to the budget of the european union, i think that the decision you have taken is extremely questionable. mr michel raymond has been convicted of fraud against the budget of the european union by the french court of cassation. you were seized by the national authorities in a perfectly lawful manner. and i am told that you did not simply wish to 'take note', as the 1976 act calls for, of the dismissal of mr michel raymond, on the grounds that you fear a lengthy appeal to the european court of first instance, as mr le pen did. simply, in the jean-marie le pen case, which has certain aspects parallel to the case before us today, the court of first instance of the european union had the opportunity to rule very clearly on 10 april 2003, interpreting the 1976 act and article 7 (4) of our rules of procedure on which you relied. the court of first instance, in its judgment of 10 april 2003, stated that the power of verification which the european parliament has when it is required to 'act' applies 'even before the date of the resignation', and therefore the date of the vacancy of the seat. article 7 of the rules of procedure provides for referral to the committee responsible by the president of parliament 'when the competent authorities of the member states initiate proceedings which may lead to the termination of the mandate of a member of the european parliament'. i therefore think, mr president, that it was your duty, in accordance with the 1976 act, our rules of procedure and the case law of the court of first instance, to take note of the termination of the mandate of mr michel raymond and not to refer it to the committee on legal affairs.

the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the resolution tabled today is based on the debate in the committee on economic and monetary affairs on the annual report on competition policy for 2002. i would like to thank mr della vedova very much for his important work. i would also like to emphasize, mr president, how much i appreciate and need the excellent cooperation with the parliamentary committees, first of all the committee on economic and monetary affairs. the resolution proposed reflects very well, in my view, the support of this committee for the commission's competition policy. i would like to take this opportunity to recall briefly where competition policy stands today and to give you an idea of the direction we would like to take in the immediate future. as you know, the current commission's mandate has set out and largely completed the reform of the whole of the competition rules. the common objective of the various elements of the reform was to make our control activities more effective and to eliminate unnecessary administrative burdens, without, however, substantially weakening the competition rules. i believe that this can help to increase competitiveness, growth and employment in europe. i should like to say a few words about each of the three main areas of competition policy: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. in the field of antitrust, at the end of 2002, the council adopted regulation 1/2003 establishing a new framework for the application of articles 81 and 82 of the ec treaty. this regulation opens a new chapter in the application of community competition rules. it is the biggest antitrust reform since 1962 and will come into effect on may 1st. these are the two main aspects of the new system: it abolishes the system of notification for agreements between undertakings and creates uniform conditions under which undertakings will operate within the common market. the application of the community competition rules becomes the rule which will enable firms to make plans much more easily than under the present system, in which agreements between firms are governed by 25 national laws in addition to community provisions. at the same time, the new system relieves firms of the burdensome notification burden and enables the commission to concentrate its full resources on prosecuting the most serious infringements of the competition rules. the reform mobilises the full potential of national competition authorities and national courts to help enforce european antitrust rules. a network of 25 national authorities is being set up, which will allow for a better and more effective division of tasks between the commission and the national authorities; the commission will have the somewhat demanding task of ensuring that the rules are applied consistently. we could go into a lot more detail, but i'm not going to do that now. however, i would like to highlight one aspect of this competition policy which will be more proactive, less based on waiting for notifications and more on the commission and the national competition authorities taking their own initiative; we have wanted to give a special role to consumers, who are the ultimate recipients and beneficiaries of our competition policy, for example by introducing a number of mechanisms to involve consumer associations more closely in the investigation of competition cases and also by encouraging their complaints. i now come to the second part of our reform, which concerns merger control. i would first like to point out that this control is not as interventionist as it might appear at first sight. the commission does not intend to prevent the restructuring of markets. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the power to adopt implementing acts in order to ensure that the commission is able to take account of the need to ensure that the rules on competition are respected. in fact, if we look at the data, we find that since 1990, out of over 2200 mergers notified to the commission, the commission has blocked 18 of them: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the merger is not blocked. the recently adopted reform of the merger regulation introduces a certain degree of flexibility in the examination times for transactions, reinforces the one-stop shop principle to the great advantage of firms and specifies that the essential criterion for assessing transactions is that of all types of adverse situations, whether it is the dominant position of a single firm or the effects of an oligopoly situation which could harm consumers' interests. as regards the commission's internal organisation, we have introduced a number of rather profound innovations in the competition sector, which have been followed and encouraged very closely by a number of honourable members, including the increased emphasis on economic analysis in the assessment of competition cases. since september 2003, the directorate-general for competition has had a new chief competition economist, who has given new impetus to the presence of economic analysis in our decision-making process. i shall now turn briefly to the third area of competition policy, namely the control of state aid. on several occasions parliament and the council have rightly insisted that the overall amount of state aid should be reduced and that, at the same time, state aid should be more focused on supporting horizontal objectives rather than supporting, often artificially, certain sectors or individual undertakings. as you know, parliament supported this step: in july 2001, we set up a framework for evaluating state aid, a scoreboard, and the latest data, published last spring, confirmed a downward trend in the level of aid. we shall see in the next edition, this april, whether this trend will continue. in the case of state aid, as i said earlier, in the case of antitrust and mergers, we have also tried to refocus the commission's work on those aspects which can be most harmful to competition in europe. we still have an intensive programme of work, between now and the end of this commission's mandate, in the state aid sector, which focuses on three main aspects: more effective changes to working procedures and methods; simplification of the methods for dealing with less significant aid cases; the commission has also proposed that the existing substantive state aid rules be revised. work on the reform of procedures is well advanced: we are preparing a regulation laying down the rules for the application of the council's rules of procedure and we want to develop new instruments for the simplified treatment of aid which does not raise significant competition problems. as a follow-up to the commission's green paper on services of general economic interest, which has been of great interest to this parliament, high priority will be given to clarifying the control mechanism concerning the payment of compensation for the costs of providing services of general economic interest. i would like to stop here and take a look at the time i have been given, but not before i have pointed out for a few seconds, mr president, how much, again with the support of parliament, we have done in this period for the international dimension of competition policy, both by further deepening certain bilateral cooperation between antitrust authorities, primarily with those of the united states of america, and by launching with other partners the first multilateral form of competition policy, the international competition network. we hope that in this area the governance of globalisation is flourishing, and not withering away, as unfortunately happens in other areas. i am of course available to listen and possibly make some comments on the speeches which will follow.
- mr president, i shall deal with one point only: state aid for services of general interest. i am speaking in particular to you, commissioner. in its resolution of 14 january, parliament has just confirmed its willingness to legislate in this area. we therefore feel that it is urgent for the commission to say clearly 'yes, we are going to prepare a legal act on codecision'. the aim is to strengthen the choice and action capacity of public authorities, particularly local and regional authorities, and to ensure that internal market and competition rules are compatible with the inalienable rights in services of general interest. to this end, we want to establish common principles, criteria for specifying exemptions and derogations from the competition rules and for financing. and we already have a codecision power, with article 95 interpreted in the light of article 16 and the charter. the draft constitutional treaty also seeks to strengthen this power. i would remind you that the commission must implement the ex post rules, but above all it must not decide ex ante itself. this is the responsibility of the treaty, the court of justice and the legislator. we are concerned about the commission's abuse of power in the name of its competition powers and we consider that there is some legal confusion, particularly as regards funding. first, you do not have to say whether the funding is legitimate or not and in particular to decide what is aid or not. only after the rule has been set do you need to ensure compatibility with competition. so there is bound to be a potential area of conflict between the legislator and you. therefore, following the altmark judgment, we ourselves want to clarify the conditions under which financial compensation for public service obligations does not fall within the scope of the state aid rules. you want to interpret the altmark yourself by means of a communication, and we want to do so by means of a legislative act. secondly, the commission, after empowering the council, may decide to implement a regulation exempting state aid from notification. in fact, services of general interest are increasingly taking on an economic dimension. but our resolution refuses to allow you to use article 86 (3) to decide everything yourselves, thus invoking an emergency that has been denied for many years. we therefore ask you to provide for a temporary derogation so that the co-decision procedure can later specify the general conditions for validation. thirdly, in view of the disputes already existing between your services and the bodies responsible for services of general interest, we are justified in asking you to respect our decision that services such as health, social housing and social services are to be excluded from the scope of the competition rules and are subject to commission control only in cases of apparent abuse of discretion. i would also like to draw your attention to the fact that we want the future codecision act to establish a right to self-production, so that the threat of interference by the commission is not constantly raised under the pretext of distortion of competition.

remind you that galileo is simply a gigantic clock, made up of some 30 satellites, which gives an extremely precise positioning in time and space. unlike gps and glonass, this is a project that must remain purely civilian. the services it will provide are very important, particularly in the field of the environment. as a tool for nature protection, it will help to locate pollution from dangerous products, icebergs, and map oceans and sea levels. it will help monitor the atmosphere, the ionosphere, radio communications, space science and even predict earthquakes or track endangered species. developments will be made in the fields of transport and communications. the fundamental contribution of galileo should be underlined, as it becomes a spearhead of our european space policy by further integrating the roles of the union and esa. and in the european research area, significant funding is provided in fp6 by the artes programme of esa and by private partners. it should be noted that - mr president, it can be assumed that the laschet report was inspired by good intentions: to strengthen the role of the united nations and to increase europe's weight in it. but it must be admitted that the proposed method is contrary to both these objectives. articles 10 to 12, the heart of the resolution, propose to inflate the security council and weaken the current veto system by replacing it with a requirement for a double veto on the core issue of threats to peace, chapter 7. this is to take account of the two basic rules that determine the effectiveness of the system, the limited number of members and the veto power of each permanent member. as for europe's weight, it is difficult to see how it could be strengthened by halving the number of its permanent members in the security council. this is what the proposal to make the european union a permanent member implies, 'as soon as its legal personality has been recognised'. this necessarily unique seat would be occupied by the famous european foreign minister, who would no longer have the right of veto. the twofold characteristic of the proposal before us is to make the existing system more complicated and weaker. this is the community method applied to the united nations. so we cannot support it. we shall, however, vote in favour of amendment no 1, a common sense amendment proposed by our british friends.
- mr president, today we are awarding the sakharov prize to mr kofi annan, as a sign of our full support for the un. and this rare moment gives me the opportunity to call to mind neglected cases or lost causes. one of these causes is respect for international law, which mr annan has defended with all the integrity of his office and his spirit, despite the american pressure cooker. the war did take place, but it was illegitimate and discredited in its motives. the subsequent revelations of the false and false charges against iraq, a posteriori, should comfort those who denounce the ecological dangers of our planet more than stocks of weapons that are massively invisible. another voice that is constantly being suppressed and covered up is that of indigenous peoples, the last survivors of ancient civilizations, but who have fundamentally acquired the values of ecology and understand their interdependencies much better than we do. too much virtue and authenticity for peoples who, in our materialistic and superficial world, could not defend even their basic rights. let us denounce this marginalization of the rights of indigenous peoples and let us make the union and the un promise to maintain the working group on indigenous peoples of the un subcommission on the promotion and protection of human rights.
- mr president, this debate on the excellent report by our colleague mr laschet and the award of the sakharov prize to the secretary-general of the united nations show the european parliament's increasingly clear desire to reaffirm the unique and irreplaceable role of the un in world international relations, in line with the millennium declaration and the commission's communication. moreover, the resolution we are about to vote on also sets out in detail and precisely the way relations between the union and the un should be conducted. there are many proposals, which i share, both with regard to strengthening the role of the european union within a stronger united nations, for example a seat on the security council, and with regard to strengthening cooperation between the institutions of the union and the united nations system. these reform proposals are ambitious, since ultimately the european union would see itself as the secular arm of the un or the eldest daughter of the un, as the eldest daughter of the church was once said about a country i know well. article 17 even envisages that the european union should play a pioneering role in defining un policy. that's good. however, behind these encouraging and dynamic projects lie questions that are worrisome as long as they are not resolved. in particular, the place and role of the most important member of the un, the united states. what can the un/eu tandem do in the face of american unilateralism, in the face of their opposition to the international criminal court, to the kyoto protocol, in the face of their willingness to use their military force alone and freely, whenever they feel their security is threatened? the un and the eu together have a long way to go before the un can really exercise the credible multilateral international authority that the world needs.
council. mr president, this morning’s debate has made clear the parliament’s strong interest in enhancing the european union’s engagement with the united nations. the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, and in particular the rapporteur, mr laschet, are to be commended on the production of this report. i fully subscribe to the statement in the report that 'the success of global governance, in the face of the challenges posed by growing globalisation and interdependence, can only be based on an effective and fair multilateral system unequivocally anchored in the united nations'. the council is firmly and formally committed to effective multilateralism in its external action. a rules-based international order with the united nations at its heart is a central element of the european security strategy, which the european council adopted in december 2003. i can assure you that council, under the irish presidency, is determined to work towards a more effective collective response to today’s threats. we are all keenly aware that terrorism and weapons of mass destruction are threats that present serious challenges, but global stability is also threatened by endemic poverty and lack of development, as well as the scourge of hiv/aids and other infectious diseases. these are hugely destabilising factors that will literally destroy the prospects of many countries if they are not effectively remedied. yesterday i told secretary-general annan that, in implementing the european security strategy, the european union will work particularly closely with the un to enhance mutual cooperation on conflict prevention and crisis management. we agreed that we would work closely on devising better planning and best-practice models for conflict prevention and post-conflict peace building. we will base this on both our organisations' experiences in these policy areas. this will involve working together on the practical implementation of the joint declaration on eu-un cooperation in crisis management signed late in 2003. we also discussed how best to build on the successful deployment in 2003 of operation artemis in the democratic republic of the congo. before this presidency ends we are aiming to have up to 1500 military personnel available to be deployed as an eu rapid reaction capability at the disposal of the secretary-general for crisis management operations. mr annan is very supportive of this valuable resource becoming available as soon as possible. i assured the secretary-general that the european union was fully behind his efforts to find – to use his words – a credible and convincing collective answer to the challenges of our time. the union will therefore support the work of the high-level panel on threats, challenges and change. i believe that the european union can make an important contribution to this highly relevant debate. the presidency appreciates the enthusiastic support of the commission in this endeavour and the work presently under way. the secretary-general has made clear his view that any changes must be a means to an end, not an end in themselves. the united nations must show, in practical and concrete ways, that it is capable of fulfilling the first purpose laid down in the charter, which is to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace. developing our rapid reaction capability in the coming months will be a demonstration of this union's willingness to contribute and to assist the un in this important area of activity. today’s debate is timely. given the challenges to the multilateral system that secretary-general annan has placed in the spotlight in such a determined way – including last friday at the world economic forum in davos – the central thrust of this report, which reaffirms support for a strong, reformed un at the centre of the multilateral system, is very welcome. this confirms that the secretary-general, the council, and the commission have the support of the people’s representatives in parliament in this endeavour. the report clearly articulates the need for the european union to 'punch its weight' at the united nations. european union member states are, collectively, major financial contributors to the united nations, contributing almost 40% of its budget. the european union will, as the report notes, represent some 450 million people from 1 may 2004. the council agrees fully that the eu needs to develop a commensurate political profile. the general thrust of the report strengthens the council in its engagement with the united nations. i wish to assure you that one of the aims of the irish presidency is to make the eu more focused, more flexible and more responsive at the united nations. i am determined that we will devote more effort to engaging with our international partners on these important questions, in the interests of both the un and the eu. effective multilateralism will be a subject of discussion at all our summits with strategic partners during this presidency. today’s discussion has highlighted a number of varied and interesting points which reflect the scope, detail and ambition of the report. we have read and heard many proposals, some of which can be endorsed immediately. some others, it would be fair to say, will need to be discussed over time. the proposal that the presidency inform the parliament of the content of the eu priorities for each un general assembly session seems an excellent idea, and the council will act on this. the proposal for exchanges of views between high-level un officials and the committees of the parliament is also to be commended. the question of eu representation at the united nations will certainly need to be addressed in the light of the final outcome of the negotiations on the constitution, which will confer a legal personality on the european union. some of the issues raised are much more complex, and merit careful consideration. i wish to commend the ambition of the report for the range of proposals that it contains concerning the activity of the parliament in relation to the various funds, programmes and agencies of the united nations. no doubt this is work that the committee concerned and the parliament will advance over time. i have also noted carefully what was said regarding the representation of the eu in the security council. clearly, this is not an issue that can be easily resolved at the moment. it must be kept under review as our common policies develop over time. likewise, the issue of the reform of the security council is not one that can be easily resolved. the high-level panel appointed by the secretary-general will address this question, among others. we are all aware of the difficulties and problems encountered by advocates of institutional reform in the un. the necessary consensus remains difficult to develop. this, however, must not deflect us from the essential task of making the security council, and the multilateral system as a whole, more effective in meeting the challenges of today’s world. again, let me reiterate my appreciation of this initiative. it has provided a stimulus for the ongoing discussion of the eu’s support for the un and the parliament’s role in that regard. i can assure you that the council is firmly aware of the issues that are addressed in it, and of the issues that have been raised here today.
