in writing. - the laschet report on relations between the european union and the un was presented in a solemn way, and its importance was highlighted by the award of the sakharov prize to kofi annan. it is in fact involved in the establishment of 'off-the-ground diplomacy', supported by a network of organisations that are only loosely controlled by national democracies. the intentions expressed (multilateralism for the method, respect for human rights, preservation of peace, conservation of nature for the substance) certainly seem excellent. but how will democratic controls be exercised? the laschet report is constantly limiting the scope for action of the member states in the un, replacing them with the european union, controlled by the european parliament, which takes advantage of this to gain the upper hand. but this is tantamount to saying that we prefer 'democracies of weak substance', such as european democracy, to national democracies with real content. in particular, the laschet report welcomes the reforms that the european constitution, if adopted, would bring about, including the union's legal personality and the european foreign minister, which would make it possible to implement this programme. this is one more reason to reject both the constitution and the laschet report.
in writing. - yes to the report's call for a more active eu role in the un. the 'multilateralism which remains the best way to achieve global peace and security' is indeed one of the safeguards against the supremacy of a superpower. but the goals that are being set are far removed from the realities and dangers of today. declarations of intent are no longer enough: poverty eradication, human development, conflict prevention, peacebuilding require financial and political investment that is up to the challenge. after the us military intervention and occupation of iraq, the negation - to the point of extinction? - of the palestinian people, the spirit which prevailed in the creation of the united nations, the principles of the charter are being abused more than ever, and even trampled underfoot by some countries. the defence of international law and the right of peoples to self-determination must be renewed more than ever and followed by action. i am thinking in particular of the effective implementation of the un peace plan for western sahara until the organisation of a referendum on self-determination, whatever the hesitations of the moroccan government now. i also think that there should be real sanctions for human rights violations and environmental damage.

in writing. - (fr) i voted against the laschet report on the draft constitution, which has not yet been adopted, in order to underline the longstanding ambitions of the eu institutions in the field of foreign policy, namely to make the eu a fully-fledged international actor as soon as the eu is recognised as a legal person in the constitution (paragraph 10). it means making it an international partner on an equal footing with a state and with all the rights of a state, including even a seat as a permanent member of the un. i would add that today's ceremony looked like a pact of mutual support between institutions trying to give each other legitimacy. although the laschet report avoids, of course, going into detail about what is to happen to the seats of france and the united kingdom on the security council, it is clear that the system proposed in the report will result in their being abolished sooner or later. although the draft constitution does not stipulate that the eu must have a single representative on the international scene, it establishes the legal conditions for this. consequently, it is highly hypocritical to support the constitution and at the same time claim that france will remain a permanent member of the un.
in writing. - (fr) the the laschet report gives the impression that it should be a champion of multilateralism in international relations. it is recommended that the un should be given a central role in this objective and that the eu's role in the un should be strengthened. but the method recommended for achieving these noble goals is wrong. the report calls for a more effective un, an enlarged security council, fewer restrictions on the right to veto decisions and more means of intervention, including military means. as with the eu, they are trying to involve us in an institutional debate in order to make us forget the fundamental problem, which is that free competition is what determines the eu's policy in the first place and that the great powers claim the right to decide alone what deserves or does not deserve the economic or military intervention of the un. the fight against terrorism is considered to be a top priority, whereas the fight against the greenhouse effect, aids or poverty is merely a formality. the un imposed sanctions on iraq, but it lets the palestinians, the chechens and many others sail their own sea. finally, the report is framed as if the european constitution had been ratified and it is claimed that an eu foreign minister can represent a european consensus on international issues. it's irresponsible. for all these reasons we have voted against the report.
in writing. - (fr) every time parliament presents a report on the foreign policy of the european union, the federalist majority in this parliament cannot resist the temptation to add points which are completely irrelevant and which in the end undermine all the work done. although we fully agree with the rapporteur on certain points, in particular the strengthening of relations between the un's internal bodies, it is inconceivable that the eu's participation as a full member of the un security council and the general assembly would be accepted or, in the same context, that the eu's foreign minister, whose functions are defined in the draft constitutional treaty for europe, should occupy the place proposed for the eu. while it is interesting to note that such proposals reveal the true nature of the federalist project, because it assumes by definition that the eu becomes a state, it is also clear that they are the product of imagination. a single observation is sufficient to show how inappropriate this idea is. what would the eu representative have proposed during the iraq crisis, when the eu was more divided than ever?
in writing. - (fr) i support the objective of a single european airspace, which should improve traffic flow and air traffic management, together with air traffic safety. however, we think that the agreement on the single european sky, which was reached by means of the conciliation procedure, is unsatisfactory in several respects. the compromise on civil and military cooperation is problematic, for example. is it necessary to point out that this is contrary to the principle of subsidiarity? military matters are not the responsibility of the eu but of the member states, which have their own defence policy and international obligations. member states must be free to organise their rights over their airspace as they see fit. as regards the creation and modification of functional airspace blocks, i am pleased that it will be the responsibility of the member states concerned with technical assistance from eurocontrol. it is important that the member states retain their right to take the final decision. we must not forget that the single european sky must not impede civil aviation as a public service or the safety of european airspace. security must not be sacrificed to the pursuit of ever greater profits.
in writing. - (fr) we are not entirely satisfied with the results of the conciliation procedure between parliament and the council on the single european sky. the texts we are voting on are merely compromises between a liberal philosophy and safety requirements, not to mention the prospect of a single european airspace, organised and managed by european public services. we have supported and made known the work of the european trade unions from the outset. they have tirelessly defended the public interest against the commercialisation of airspace. by mobilising their forces and working hard, they introduced the principle of non-separation of technical services and ensured that member states retained responsibility for the functional airspace blocks. finally, they got the commission to commit itself to publishing an evaluation of the directive within five years. without these concessions from the council, it would have looked much worse. however, in the light of the liberalisation of the other transport sectors, we are still very concerned about the future of public control of this sector, where competition is fierce. the agreement also allows member states to decide whether to entrust air traffic control to a public service or to a private company. because of these concerns, we have not voted in favour of the outcome of the conciliation procedure.
in writing. (fr) two directives are being amended today. the first concerns the coordination of procedures for the award of public supply, public service and public works contracts, and the second concerns the coordination of procedures for the award of contracts for water, energy, transport and postal services. these changes, based on the principles of free competition in an open market, are in our view worrying, as they come at a time when france is moving towards greater decentralisation and national review of public procurement contracts. we want to ensure that the public services concerned will continue to cover the same geographical area and provide the same services. we therefore vote against these two directives.

- mr president, mr secretary-general, thank you for your wonderful speech which rings true and puts each country face to face with its responsibilities. we are honoured by your highly symbolic presence in our assembly and we in turn respectfully and emotionally greet the relatives of mr vieira de mello and the other victims of the heinous terrorist attack in baghdad. one year ago, mr secretary-general, almost to the day, the european parliament adopted a resolution in support of the mission of united nations inspectors in iraq. many of us still wanted to believe that it was possible to avoid the war, which we felt was devastating. in the period since then, an unprecedented link has emerged between world public opinion and the united nations. in the streets, millions of our fellow citizens were mobilizing, while in the security council the majority of member countries were resisting and fighting. here and there, the aim was the same: to try to prevent a bloody, destabilising and irresponsible adventure. rarely, as in those days, has the un been so true to the opening words of the charter: "we the peoples of the united nations". we didn't succeed, but the lesson paid off. a certain idea of world organization was, of course, seriously flouted by a coalition of states, but it has been spectacularly validated by collective experience since then, to the point that yesterday's warring parties are now calling for the un. the idea is that war is definitely not the way to solve the world's problems. secondly, no nation, no matter how super-powered, can ignore the global challenges facing the international community. finally, the building of a world of peace cannot be limited to a mobilisation against terrorist networks. if, unfortunately, the tragic impasse in the middle east continues - mr president, the cooperation system between the european union and the acp countries is characterized by two opposing developments. on the one hand, the sustainability of the original institutions set up by the lomé conventions and confirmed by the cotonou convention, notably the joint parliamentary assembly, is more alive than ever, and our colleague colette flesch's report highlights the innovative developments that the joint assembly experienced in 2003, but at the same time the objectives and the content of the cooperation these institutions are supposed to implement tend to weaken, to be depleted, to be trivialised, to be fragmented, to be dissolved, to the point that there is a risk that they will soon cease to exist, if things are left to run their course, than a ceiling on financial aid and free trade agreements that could be a source of more difficulty for the acp countries than for their real development aid instruments. as the rapporteur points out, the creation in 2003 of three standing committees, including an economic development committee to monitor the very sensitive issue of the negotiation of future partnership agreements, reinforces the permanence of the parliamentary assembly and improves the quality of its work. the system of co-rapporteurs is original and the work in committee makes it possible to reach more restricted, more elaborate, better prepared, less routine resolutions, which give rise to much more in-depth debates than could be achieved in plenary. but while the institutional framework is being strengthened and refined, the future of the cooperation instruments themselves is questionable. if future economic partnership agreements merely apply the principle of equality of competitors, are they not likely to create insurmountable cash problems for the acp countries by causing them to lose a large part of their customs revenue, i.e. a large and sometimes essential part of their budget? secondly, is it not true that the direct competition of community goods and local production without adequate safeguards is likely to weaken or even stifle many sectors of activity in the acp countries? if we are to help avoid these diversions, the unique north-south parliamentary forum of the joint assembly must ensure that the major negotiation of the partnership agreements is conducted with the necessary ambition and energy, particularly in the field of agriculture, which is the foundation of development. the acp countries will only have a sufficiently strong agriculture if it is adequately protected as a nascent industry in its take-off phase. the cotonou framework, that of regional economic zones, can be considered the most appropriate to promote the establishment of homogeneous regional common markets with a common external tariff. it is by working together in this direction, mr president, that acp and european countries will no longer find themselves in different camps in future negotiations on agriculture and world trade.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the own-initiative report on agricultural incomes is intended to help to bring about a step back in the implementation of the european agricultural model, which is based on the multifunctionality and competitiveness of farms. income is the relevant barometer of farm viability. without sufficient income, farmers disappear and production moves away from the most fragile areas. if farmers are eliminated and concentrations accelerate, we risk going against the european model we advocate, which implies the presence of farmers in all the territories. the income analysis is therefore clearly of interest. the following are the useful observations for the period 1995-2002. first, average agricultural income in the eu-15 increased by 7% with large national variations, for example, up 32% in portugal and down 30% in the uk. secondly, public support accounts for more than 50% of this result, but its distribution is questionable. 20% of farms receive 73% of the aid for 59% of the area and 25% of the employment. thirdly, producer prices fell by 1.1% while consumer prices rose by 11%. fourthly, the slight improvement in this average income is due to the fact that the cake is being shared by fewer and fewer farmers, since the labour force in this sector decreased by 15,7% over the period considered. the question is: can we let this continue without risking our european model of agriculture? this is all the more serious as the application of multi-functionality will lead to higher production costs, while public support is set to decline by 2013 for farmers in the 15 member states, due in particular to the increase in community support for agriculture in the 10 new countries. this situation cannot leave the european union indifferent. the future direction of the cap should be considered in order to make it consistent with the two objectives of multi-functionality and competitiveness assigned to agricultural holdings. in this perspective, the market must tend to remunerate the act of agricultural production. public support must increasingly be used to compensate for the non-market services that agriculture provides to society. the latest reform of the cap has made positive progress in this respect, in particular through the conditionality and modulation of aid. but with decoupling, the cap establishes historical rights acquired which will de facto prohibit the remuneration of multifunctionality for all farms in all territories. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. as regards market-generated revenues, i advocate giving priority to price and market policy, considering that improvements in product quality, however necessary, are only the passport to access these markets. as a result, several directions must be opened or reaffirmed in order for the market to play its role in avoiding the collapse of prices and thus incomes. i quote them: 'the regulation of supply which is flexible and adapted to production; the introduction of safety filters, capped by production; the community's encouragement of the contractual policy of the sectors for a better sharing of added value; the submission of our imports to the same standards as those of the union'. ladies and gentlemen, everyone will understand from this report that there is still a great deal of progress to be made in order to enable the cap to achieve its objectives. our european agricultural model is legitimate in its design. he has to become one again in reality. that is why i regret the commissioner's absence from this debate all the more.
- mr president, this report is a welcome initiative and i congratulate its author. in fact, it is taking stock of agricultural income just before the implementation of the cap reform and the enlargement of the european union. it will therefore serve as a reference document for us in a few years' time when we meet again, i hope, in this house to assess the effects of the reform on the incomes of our farmers. will the accession of ten new countries, themselves heavily agricultural, and the alignment of european agricultural prices with world prices bring us a happy tomorrow? i don't want to play the cassandras, but unfortunately, i doubt it. this report highlights important facts, in particular the 7% increase in european agricultural income over seven years, which hides many disparities between regions and sectors of activity and is based on a deterioration of the european agricultural model, as the rapporteur also pointed out in his speech. in ten years, a quarter of european farmers have disappeared, farms have grown and production has intensified. french small farmers have incomes so low that in france the government offers them access to the minimum income of integration, a social support system reserved for the poorest. i come from the vosges, a rural department near here. between 1988 and 2000, the number of farms in the region fell by 40% and the number of dairy farms halved. at the same time, the area of farms increased by 65% and the number of cows per farm by 30%. this concentration of agriculture is the undermining of the european family farming model, which the parliamentary report also highlights very well. decoupled aid is not a viable solution for the farmer. according to the study by inra of nantes, partial decoupling would result in a reduction of up to 32% of the simulated income of an intensive dairy farmer in 2008, as decoupled aid will not compensate for the 20% decrease in the milk price foreseen for 2006-08. the report was prepared by consulting various experts on the subject. all of them stressed this inherent paradox of the latest reform of the common agricultural policy. how can we conceive of increasing costs due to multifunctionality and at the same time demanding a reduction in agricultural prices by aligning european prices with world prices? what is the solution for farmers caught between rising production costs and falling prices? no expert could tell us that. finally, the report describes a risk which is of particular concern to me. this is the ecological conditionality of aid for small farms, as their income will increasingly depend on aid, especially with decoupling. a small farmer who fails to comply with one of the many directives - including the birds directive - would therefore lose his income and his aid. this will reduce the incomes of farmers who are already fragile and whose investment capacity is low. this report points to the painful aspects of the common agricultural policy and its latest reform, and i can only welcome the fact that these facts are being brought to light. however, some parts of this report remain ambiguous and i cannot endorse them. i cannot ask the member states, and i quote, 'that partial decoupling be effectively applied', since i have always been opposed to any kind of decoupling, whether partial or total. in the same vein, i am not, and i quote, 'in favour of rebalancing in favour of the second pillar'. the first pillar, which ensures that farmers can keep a profitable price for their agricultural products, cannot be weakened to subsidize the second pillar. this parliamentary report has the merit of clearly presenting important and unfortunately painful facts for the common agricultural policy. however, it provides ambiguous support for key elements of the cap reform that my group has spoken out against, and that is why i will find it very difficult to support it.
- mr president, - since your seat is vacant, i cannot unfortunately add 'commissioner fischler' - the interest of this own-initiative report on the development of agricultural incomes in the european union lies more in the questions it raises than in the elements of solution it would like to provide. his departure is undeniable. we can make all the noise we want about the european agricultural model - the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. the socioeconomic consequences of management measures adopted on such a fragile basis are, however, significant, since the survival of fisheries, of the whole fisheries industry, is at stake. the scientific effort must therefore be strengthened and cover both marine biology, selection of fishing gear and the socioeconomic consequences of resource management measures. it is essential to change the present imbalance in the common fisheries policy, which does not take account, in general, of the dual objective of conserving resources and renewing fishing opportunities. to this end, the future regional advisory councils will play a leading role in the preparation of requests for scientific opinions. they shall require a range of management options, accompanied by an assessment of their biological and socioeconomic implications. such a development should make it possible to move from a brutal and irreversible action to a gradual, progressive, flexible and constantly adaptable action. i am glad that the amendments i tabled in this area have been adopted.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. first of all, i should like to thank mr souchet for the detailed report on the recovery plan for the northern hake. the council discussed the recovery plan for hake in december 2003 and also accepted some of the amendments contained in the report. the first is that we have now removed fishing effort from the proposal. the second is that we have reduced the stock size corresponding to the precautionary approach from 143 000 tonnes to 140 000 tonnes and that we have reduced the minimum stock size from 103 000 to 100 000 tonnes, as recommended by the scientists. despite these changes, the objective remains the same. the aim is to bring the stock of northern hake to a safe biological level and this involves a number of measures. first of all, we must establish a minimum stock size below which, according to scientific assessments, the stock would be in danger of collapse. this includes guidelines on tacs or tacs based on the scientific advice we receive. the tac shall be set at precautionary levels unless it leads to a decrease in biomass in a year. if the stock size falls below the minimum level, the council must reduce the tac. in any case, the tac should not be altered by more than 15% from one year to the next. finally, the proposal also contains measures to improve the control of vessels fishing for northern hake and also rules on the prior notification of landings: if more than two tonnes of hake are landed, this can only be done in dedicated ports, and there are also stricter storage and transport conditions. so much for the proposal. i shall then be voting on the proposed amendments at the end. thank you. thank you.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, you are here and we are very pleased to have you. the commission's proposal to establish a plan for the recovery of the northern hake stock falls within the scope of the new provisions provided for in the framework regulation reforming the cfp. this new system, which is in principle aimed at particularly threatened species, is combined with a new instrument, management by fishing effort, which is in addition to the instruments already in place, in particular the fixing of tacs and quotas. after the 'cabillaud' recovery plan, the 'merlu du nord' plan is the second of its kind proposed by the commission. it is in fact the second link in a long chain, since since its submission parliament has been given two new plans with exactly the same structure. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing opportunities for cod, haddock and sole in the bay of biscay and the channel are not exceeded. this point must be emphasised, especially since it appears that when a fishing undertaking exploits stocks subject to different recovery plans, it is obliged to comply with the provisions of all the recovery plans concerned, both for catches from stocks to be recovered and for catches from stocks of associated species. this is particularly clear from the written reply you have just given me, commissioner, on 9 february to a question i had put to you. this is a particularly heavy burden for the fishermen, especially in areas where the commission intends to superimpose multiple recovery plans applied to virtually all the species caught, and i am thinking in particular of those in the bay of biscay. the commission had originally planned to merge the stocks of cod and northern hake, two species with very different characteristics. this inappropriate link was, fortunately, later dissolved. our committee drew up its report after extensive consultation with the professional circles concerned, in particular at a hearing held in brussels on 25 november last, bringing together representatives of french, spanish and british professional organizations. the latter particularly regretted that they had not been seriously involved in the preparation of the recovery plan and in the assessment of the state of the resource on which it is based, contrary to the provisions of the new framework regulation and contrary to the requirement made by our parliament, in particular in its opinion on the integration of environmental protection requirements into the cfp. we were told that the regional workshop organised by the commission was more like a notification of decisions already taken than a real consultation meeting, prior to any decision. the trade unions also stressed the imbalance in the basis of the commission's proposal. this is based exclusively on biological considerations and is not accompanied by any impact study on the socio-economic consequences of the proposed plan. however, it is clear that the drastic reduction of tacs planned at the very beginning of the plan is not compatible with the sustainability of the companies involved in the northern hake fishery. the trade representatives also expressed their reservations about the effectiveness and applicability of the system of reducing fishing effort, whether by the system of days at sea or kilowatt days. they expressed concern that the overlapping of a new management instrument with the tac and quota system and the specific management measures already adopted would end up undermining the principle of relative stability and contribute to an increase in discards. they also questioned the effectiveness of a fishing effort reduction scheme in achieving the desired result in terms of improving the stock. in fact, we have no scientific assessment from ices on this issue that would guarantee that a reduction in effort leads to an effective reduction in the catch per fishery. nor do we have the evaluation of the transitional measures for the restoration of stocks taken under annex 17 of the regulation fixing tacs and quotas for 2003. the extremely complex formula for reducing effort also poses serious problems of fairness and predictability for member states. it also establishes a uniform and rigid system, applied in virtually identical fashion from one stock to another, which does not take account of the specific characteristics of the various community fleets, in particular their frequent versatility. your committee on fisheries considered that the multiannual approach adopted to address the question of the management of the stock of northern hake is fully justified and relevant. this approach has a long-term objective of preserving the site, while at the same time giving professionals the visibility and security they need to ensure the sustainability of their businesses. however, it appeared to us that the establishment of a recovery plan for northern hake was not a measure proportionate to the state of the stock concerned, as shown by the latest scientific assessments and observations of professionals. although vigilance is obviously required, the trend over the last two years shows an upturn in the level of the resource. since the stock of northern hake is not below the biological safety limits, it did not seem appropriate to include it in a recovery plan under article 5 of the framework regulation. the stock of northern hake must, according to your committee, be subject to a multiannual management plan under article 6 of the same regulation. we believe that this instrument is preferable because it is more in line with the state of the resource and will help to achieve the dual objective of sustainable conservation of the stock and conservation of fisheries. by proposing to replace the recovery plan recommended by the commission with a multiannual management plan, we are in line with the guidelines we have already adopted, which recommend that, in the management of fragile stocks, simple, flexible and permanently adaptable rules - such as multiannual tacs - be adopted, rather than uniform and complex systems with uncertain effects, such as fishing effort management systems, which have not yet proved their worth.
- mr president, on behalf of my group i have repeatedly criticised the european council's tendency to set the union new priorities while denying it the corresponding financial means. this policy of scribbling has too often led us to abandon a field which was considered crucial the day before, in favour of another which was considered decisive the next day. it was by stripping peter to clothe paul that we survived, year after year, on a ridiculous budget. in 2004, it reached a historic low of below 1% of gdp, 20% below the ceiling agreed by the fifteen for the period 2000-06. this short-sighted view of the union's responsibilities is creating an explosive situation with enlargement. if the six states that are net contributors to the european budget actually implement their plan to impose a freeze on spending at their current level from 2007, what a lot of good promises will be shattered! the major construction projects, which were quickly dubbed the 'growth initiative', are at risk of being buried once again. as for regional and social aid, the appropriations of the cohesion fund will melt like snow in the sun for the majority of their present beneficiaries and many of their future recipients. so much for cohesion! so much for solidarity! in social terms, this is cynicism, in political terms, irresponsibility. this severe judgment in favour of the states concerned does not, however, lead me to grant a satisfactory decision to the commission. your communication, mr president of the commission, is rather laconic on the choices to be made to meet the needs that are emerging. where is the announced ambition, even if the challenge of balanced development of an enlarged european union cannot of course be met by an increase in the financial perspective of one or two tenths of a percent of gdp alone? in writing. - before negotiating the financial perspective for 2007-13, it is important to define the framework for their policy orientations. in this respect, today's debate allows the commission, as it often does, to seek the support of the european parliament in order to obtain a fairly high annual resource line, at 1.24% of gross national income (and again, without the european development fund), against the position of the contributing states, including france, which would like 1% (as in 2004). this conjunction between parliament and the commission implicitly refers to the concept of a gradual increase in the union's missions, which should one day lead to a federal budget. the commission is also launching a campaign for a european tax. we must avoid any drift in this direction, so as not to feed a new bureaucracy and not to jeopardise the competitiveness objectives set in lisbon. the european union, which is at the service of the states, must not take over their tasks, including redistribution. it should only bring added value to coordination, which requires only light administration and limited resources. it must live on contributions that the nations vote on and control annually. in these circumstances, the present position of the paying states seems to us to be entirely justified.
commission. mr president, the study 'global assessment of organic contaminants in farmed salmon', published on 9 january 2004 in science magazine, compared the levels of 14 organochlorine contaminants in samples of farmed and wild salmon. besides dioxins and pcbs, the study reports on the presence of residues of organochlorine pesticides, the use of which has long been prohibited in the eu. this study does not raise new food safety issues as the levels found are consistent with the results from other surveys and from official controls. this does not, however, mean that the presence of these contaminants is not a cause for concern. as regards dioxins, strict eu maximum levels were adopted in 2001 for dioxins in feed and food, including fish. however, in setting these levels, the commission had to take into account the reality of the current background contamination of the environment in order not to endanger the food supply. i would remind you that worldwide, only the european union and korea have adopted maximum levels for dioxins in feed and food. these maximum levels are part of a comprehensive strategy adopted by the european commission in 2001 to reduce the presence of dioxins and pcbs in the environment, in feed and in food. the implementation of this strategy would give new impetus to the reduction of the background contamination. as a result, it will be possible to lower progressively the maximum levels to follow this downward trend. the legislation foresees that, as early as this year, the maximum levels have to be revised to integrate some pcbs with toxicological effects similar to dioxins. furthermore, it is foreseen that by the end of 2006 the maximum levels will be revised, aiming for a significant reduction. for the other pcbs, the european food safety authority is currently undertaking a risk assessment. the result of this risk assessment is expected to become available by the end of 2004. the commission will thereafter consider the setting of maximum levels also for these pcbs in feed and food. the organochlorine pesticides detected in the study published in science have long been banned in the european union. however, their continued presence in fish is due to the fact that they are very persistent compounds, which can still be found in the environment. the european union has established maximum levels for these pesticides in animal feed, including fish feed. on the basis of updated risk assessments undertaken by the authority, the commission will consider whether a revision of the current levels is necessary for the protection of animal and human health. the highest levels of two pesticides – toxaphene and dieldrin – found by the study in salmon feed exceed the maximum levels fixed by the eu. we have, accordingly, drawn the attention of the member states to these findings and requested that they submit data from official controls and, if necessary, reinforce those controls. finally, i would stress that the levels of dioxins reported in the study are all below the eu maximum levels. fish – be it farmed or wild – has its place in a well-balanced diet to ensure that consumers continue to benefit from its positive health effects.

in writing. mr garot (s). - (fr) i voted in favour of mr garot's excellent report and i would like to take this opportunity to congratulate him on his work on european agriculture. mr garot has managed to strike a good balance between those who want to free europe from agriculture in favour of the world market and those who see the eu budget as a 'milk-cooker' that can make the richest farmers even richer.
in writing. - (fr) i voted in favour of mr garot's report in order to recognise an initiative which has for once made it possible to open a debate on one of the fundamental questions for the maintenance of the european agricultural model, namely the income of farmers. the debate has made it possible to do away with the incoherent and technical methods which are usually imposed on us when we deal with the stream of legislative proposals from the commission. i also fully agree with the report's emphasis on the main objectives of the cap, namely 'the importance of promoting a territorial agriculture in the union which can maintain the largest possible number of farms and people employed everywhere' and 'ensuring the agricultural population of the same living conditions and stable incomes in order to maintain agriculture as a profession throughout the territory of the european union'. i can only express my surprise at the contradictory reasoning which consists in approving the commission's proposals, whether they concern the disconnection or the reduction of external protection, and in rejecting the risk of a complete falsification of the european agricultural model which these proposals involve. my support is therefore not, of course, directed at the rural decoupling and development mentioned in mr garots' report.
in writing. - (fr) it is clear that a large part of agricultural research has, in one way or another, been directed to areas where the capitalists in the food and drink industry thought they could make the greatest profit. the report recommends that at least some of the research be directed to areas which are currently neglected. it would be a good thing, although unlike the rapporteur, we do not believe that the development of so-called sustainable agriculture and so-called organic agricultural production, which he advocates, is necessarily a real benefit for the vast majority of consumers or for small family farms. we are not, of course, against such a reorientation of agricultural research or against its being financed by public funds, as the rapporteur would like. this wish underlines the inability of the market economy to secure the financing of research if the results of the research do not result in immediate profits.
in writing. - (fr) the report on the recognition of professional qualifications recommends that the scope for the provision of services be extended and qualifications harmonised in order to increase the mobility and free movement of workers in europe. the aim is to ensure the quality of the service provided by a service provider to a customer, to enable the customer to find the person responsible if he is not satisfied with the service, and to provide insurance against the risks. however, the text does not mention the rights conferred by the recognised qualifications, the guarantees offered, the status and working conditions, or the improvement of training conditions. we cannot support a policy which is designed to give guarantees to firms or customers to promote trade union mobility, and no guarantees to workers. we cannot support a policy which contributes to social dumping by creating fierce competition between wage earners without any security, and which thus undermines social status and performance. we are in favour of harmonizing qualifications, which must be inextricably linked to a definition of status, working conditions and social obligations in terms of pay and social protection, as this would promote mobility, which would result in improved living and working conditions in all european countries. we have therefore voted against mr zappalà's report.
(parliament adopted the legislative resolution) cod is an example of the fact that fisheries resources are not inexhaustible. to preserve them, the commission constantly supplies fishing efforts with various instruments for managing stocks and vessels. the depletion of stocks shall be limited by means of total allowable catches, which shall be divided into national quotas. the number of boats is being reduced continuously by means of the financial instrument for fisheries management. the council regulation of 20 december 2002 on the sustainable exploitation of fisheries resources addresses these instruments but mainly lays the foundations for a third management instrument, proposed on 27 june 2003, which sets a ceiling for fishing effort in kilowatt days. if stocks are not to fall below the biomass limit, such as 100,000 tonnes for the northern hake, the number of days that vessels are not in port must be limited in relation to their performance. apart from the complexity of this instrument, what is the point of ignoring european fishermen whose japanese, russian and other industrial fishermen are preying on the stocks thus released?
in writing. - (fr) the cercas report shows what every worker already knows, namely that employers and politicians who want a workforce that does what it is told to do also want employers to be able to set their working hours as they wish, without legal limits. the united kingdom is a leader in this field. the rapporteur says that 'more than 4 million people now work more than 48 hours a week, almost 1 million more than when the directive came into force. the number of people working more than 55 hours has also risen to over 1.55 million. 1 % of workers in the united kingdom have a weekly working time of more than 70 hours.' as regards the individual consent of the worker to work such hours, the cynicism of such a regulation is underlined by the rapporteur when he says that workers should be asked to sign declarations of consent at the same time as the conclusion of the contract of employment. so you can choose to work yourself to death or not to have a job. this general offensive against any provision on working conditions which might afford workers even the slightest protection against the omnipotence of employers is a serious social step backwards. (the minutes were suspended in accordance with rule 137 (1) of the rules of procedure)
(parliament adopted the legislative resolution) the purpose of the cercas report was to carry out a thorough review of the directive on the maximum weekly working time in the member states of the european union. it shall be set at 48 hours, measured over a period of four months. however, the directive allows for exceptions to the extension of the measurement period by calculating it on an annual basis and at the same time to disregard the rule if the employees voluntarily renounce it. the reasoning of the report acknowledges that such exceptions are becoming the rule in europe. in the united kingdom, the individual waiver clause must have been signed by one third of employees, 4 million of whom already work more than 48 hours a week. the resolution therefore asks the commission why it has not carried out the evaluation of the directive that should have been carried out in 2003. in calling for improvements in working conditions and the health of workers, particularly women, the resolution sought to limit as far as possible the number of workers who exceed the 48-hour working week and, in particular, to abolish the individual waiver of the rule, which is clearly being abused. once again the vast majority of members have shown their indifference to social issues and their concern solely for profit by voting in favour of amendments which eliminate any desire to limit working time. that is why we voted against the amended resolution.

- madam president, in this hearing before the international court of justice on the israeli security wall, the problem seems to us to be very badly posed and therefore likely to be very badly solved. the barrier is only a sub-part of a larger plan called disengagement, which is only an annex to an even broader process, the roadmap for peace negotiations. all the interlocking of these different levels is very complex. it would therefore be inappropriate to try to judge a small sub-part separately without trying to consider its role in the overall process. the eu has also been active in the fight against terrorism, particularly since it is seen as a purely legal matter, whereas it is part of a peace process which is obviously political in nature. that is why the european countries which opposed the referral of the problem to the international court of justice on the grounds that it would hinder peace efforts were perfectly right. we must not look at this problem with the narrowest of eyes and risk putting into question a peace process which everyone would rather support. finally, a distinction must be made between the principle of the safety barrier and its layout. i think i have noticed some confusion in this debate on this subject. the barrier's route may be a bargaining chip, as modifiable as any bargaining chip, but its principle is part of a state's sovereign right - and not just a state whose survival is constantly threatened - to ensure the security of its citizens.

- the next item is the statement by the commission on corporate governance and the supervision of financial services (parmalat case). i call mr bolkestein on behalf of the commission.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, after the enron affair - and this is one of the points on which i agree with theresa villiers - some in europe thought that this kind of affair was valid for american capitalism but not for european capitalism. well, with the parmalat affair, it is demonstrated that european capitalism in the 21st century can experience similar drifts. in reality, we are faced with something that goes far beyond the parmalat case and concerns the adaptation of tools that in reality have not fundamentally changed since the 19th century, while the nature of capitalism has changed so much. in the 19th century, a business confronted capital and labor. since then, however, capital has been dispersed and has found a thousand ways of intervening with great intelligence, while labour remains with its own strength, without a european or world market. we are dealing with four major problems: the question of tax havens, the question of capital structures, the question of the divorce between financing and production and, finally, the question of the fate of employees. no less than that. in this connection, i thank you, commissioner, for the proposals you have put forward, for they are a small seed planted on the long road to the regulation of world capitalism. that said, i should like to point out two or three difficulties which i think arise from the proposals you have made. i think you do not share the view of theresa villiers that it would be enough to put a policeman behind every banker to regulate capitalism. as for me, i agree with her on one point: there will always be thugs. there are problems in shipping and there always will be, just as there are problems in finance, which will always have problems. but we must not give them a free hand! today, the functioning of modern capitalism offers perches for financial thugs and in fact, these perches are called tax havens, tax fraud and illegible structures. what we have to fight is this invisibility that prevents us from arresting the culprit. this is why we must fight tax havens with determination, by exerting more pressure, by all the means at our disposal, whether it be embargoes or boycotts. if we boycott a country because it does not respect human rights, why not boycott a country because it harbours fraudulent capitalism? i think that's worth thinking about. and then, if we really want to achieve transparency, then we have to give voice to those who can have a counterweight. you cannot expect better regulation of the way businesses operate without giving employees more say. this applies to the debate we had on the report by mr giorgios katiforis on the rating agencies and it also applies to the takeovers which our parliament has dealt with. i would also like to mention the issue of company boards, and on this point, commissioner, it seems to me that the text you have submitted to us on corporate governance falls far short of what we need. in conclusion, i would like to remind you that the life of a company is too important to be left in the hands of the financiers.
mr president, for years the boss of parmalat had to speak to his 36,000 employees in 30 countries in the same language as all bosses do to their workers. they had to be told that their wages could not be increased, that staff had to be reduced and that it was the necessary competitiveness that required this. well, the workers at this company have seen the grossness of these lies. they could see that they were tricked. how many more could have been raised with the 14 billion the parmalat boss embezzled? how many supposedly necessary redundancies could have been avoided? the worst part is that all those who have been complicit in these embezzlements, the banks and the administrations, will continue as before, while the 36,000 workers of the company risk leaving their livelihood and thousands of milk farmers are harmed. but among the companies you claim to be the majority and that have an ethical and honest behaviour, how many other parmalat are not yet disclosed? and how do you know? how could the public tell the difference between the bosses who are thugs and the ones who pretend not to be? and besides the open gangsterism of the bosses of parmalat and many others, how many large companies, all of them in reality, practice this form of gangsterism - legal, that one - which consists of closing a factory by throwing its workers out the door, simply to realize an additional stock market surplus? your laws give bosses and boards of directors dictatorial power over their companies. we are for workers, consumers and the public to be able to control companies, their accounts, how they make their profits and how they use them. the community must be able to monitor them at all times and prohibit decisions which are clearly contrary to its interests. tax havens aren't just in the bahamas. to eliminate them here in europe, we must eliminate banking secrecy and business secrecy.
commission. mr president, as i said the key sentence is: 'it is clear that the time has come to put some real order here.' i mentioned three demands to be formulated: the special operations should be listed in company accounts; their purpose should be explained – why the company has them at all; and the group auditor must be responsible for checking. we are considering stronger disclosure requirements in amendments to the fourth and seventh company law directives to be adopted in september, but i do not know whether those amendments are sufficient to control the whole business of offshore tax havens and special purpose vehicles. however, these three requirements which i have just formulated certainly must be met and we must find a way of doing this.

in writing. - (fr) there is reason to welcome the new protocol which increases the resources of the international oil pollution compensation fund (iopc fund) to eur 930 million. i therefore voted in favour of the gil-robles gil-delgado report. i note, however, that the damage caused by the sinking of the prestige is estimated at at least eur 5 billion. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the oil crisis. i therefore believe that the ceiling for the replacement of the iopc fund should continue to be gradually increased and that it may be necessary for the european states to set up a supplementary fund, provided that this does not serve as a pretext for postponing the necessary adjustments to the iopc fund. it is also necessary to adopt international conventions which not only indicate the responsibility of the shipowner, as is the case today, but which extend the circle of those responsible to all the operators in the transport sector, the shipowners, the freight forwarders and, of course, the owners of the ship's cargo. the latter should therefore be encouraged to make efforts to choose safe vessels.
in writing. - (fr) the i voted in favour of this report because it is important that the present system be made more efficient in terms of compensation for victims. the supplementary fund is thus intended to ensure effective, prompt and fair compensation for future victims of oil pollution. member states should therefore sign and ratify the protocol on this fund as soon as possible. i have to express certain reservations, however. firstly, it is unacceptable that the calculation of compensation does not take account of the human, economic and environmental damage caused by the sinking of the prestige. it is also regrettable that the possibility of using a supplementary european fund (the cope fund) with a ceiling of eur 1 billion has been cut off. it could have facilitated the compensation of victims who have not been able to obtain full compensation under the international system. the project which was abandoned is a bit like the supplementary fund in question! finally, the member states should implement as soon as possible the measures proposed at european and international level following the erika and prestige disaster. finally, i would remind you that it is just as important to prevent disasters as it is to ensure a genuine preventive policy. the polluters should be punished severely and every single actor involved in the transport of goods held accountable.
(parliament adopted the legislative resolution) the parmalat company has been presented as a classic example of successful liberal globalisation. parmalat was a small family-owned pasteurised milk company which developed thanks to eu aid schemes. since 1974, the company had been able to multiply the number of subsidiaries and create shell companies in tax havens. the system survived until 11 november 2003, when auditors expressed doubts about a €500 million investment in the cayman islands. parmalat is, like enron, tyco, world com and ahold, in fact the prototype of this ruthless capitalism. for 30 years, parmalats management received public subsidies, kept accounts secret and reported fictitious profits. this practice led to the closure of several thousand jobs. the motion for a resolution does not, however, deal with this mafia practice, but is too much a statement. that is why we have chosen neither to vote for nor against. firstly, the eu should do everything possible to ensure that all those responsible are quickly extradited and brought to justice. the eu must also stop providing public subsidies to this type of enterprise. the workers and their organisations should also be provided with the means to control the accounts effectively. finally, the tax havens of the union (san marino, monaco, luxembourg, etc.) should be abolished.

outside the scope of its competence. the commission's role is to apply, not to legislate. it is also to remove the ambiguity of the treaties and the case law that our parliament is calling for a legal act in codecision which should include the principles of financing. in this respect, only codecision would make it possible to achieve a legitimate and viable compromise. in the white paper to be published before april, the commission must therefore clearly say yes or no to this request for a legislative act. by saying no, by not answering clearly and by arrogating to itself the right to impose definitions and substantive rules, it would be abusing its power. for the time being, on the basis of the information at my disposal, i find that in the package being prepared it arrogates to itself the power to lay down the rules, and that many of its choices are in formal contradiction with the european parliament's resolution. our resolution, adopted on 14 january this year, says that 'the action to be taken at community level is to ensure that they are exercised within the internal market and, in particular, to ensure that the competition rules are compatible with public service obligations'. i note that the monti package, which i have read, on the contrary, makes financing more difficult in the name of full compliance with the competition rules. i would like to stress, in these circumstances, and we have already said this to you here - i am reminded in particular of the speeches made by mr langen and mrs flautre last year - that we do not want a new communication on the interpretation of the treaty and the case law. we want the commission to prepare a legislative act leading to the codecision procedure. the commission, on the other hand, is competent to apply the rules. it is therefore justified in preparing a decision and a framework, but these executive acts depend, as everyone knows, on the interpretation of the rules. we therefore ask you to state explicitly today that, when you have corrected them after consultation, these texts in preparation will only enter into force provisionally, pending the adoption of a legislative act. i would also like to draw your attention to the substance of the monti proposals, which run counter to our resolution. far from increasing legal certainty, they would exacerbate insecurity. many services of general economic interest, especially social services, which did not notify before, now have to do so. the requirement of tendering procedures for the acceptance of compensation would be tightened. our requests for criteria for cost calculation are ignored. the concept of overcompensation would be broadly extended. as for services mainly provided to undertakings, they would be considered as not falling within the concept of a service of general economic interest, which constitutes a characteristic intrusion into the field of definitions. hence my questions. what is the commission's timetable for action? in the white paper we have asked you to present by april, will you respond consistently to the consultation and to the proposals on compensation? will you say clearly yes or no to a legal act in codecision? would you say that your implementing texts are provisional pending the adoption of a corresponding legal act?
commission. mr president, i would like to say what a pleasure it is to be here this afternoon. with several hours of further debates ahead of me, i will have been able to spend the whole day in the hemicycle, and what more could a man want – except perhaps to be lying on a beach in langkawi?! - mr president, one month after the adoption of the herzog report on services of general interest, which called for the establishment of a european legal framework adopted in codecision, we are already in a state of confusion, as the oral question by philippe herzog shows. the rapporteur finds that, at the same time, the commission was preparing on its own, under its own authority, a regulation on financial compensation for services of general interest. today the commission has only half-confessed and promised that it will wait until the consultations on the green paper are over before deciding anything. that's good. but i say to mr herzog, in the years to come you will see many more, and worse. it was simply not necessary to put one's finger in the european legal framework. this concept, like that of a framework directive, is ambiguous, because no one knows exactly what should be included, from the authorised subsidies to the definition of the service itself, including the principles of organisation, obligations and relations with users. and the notion of a legal framework respecting subsidiarity, invented by the european parliament, is even more ambiguous, even contradictory, because true subsidiarity in this area would be to accept that public services, which are indeed essential to the life of our societies, must be defined, organised and managed as closely as possible to the citizens within the national framework. we need only one rule: each state is free to decide on its public services. the corollary of this rule is that public service obligations take precedence over community competition rules.
- mr president, commissioner, i thank you for turning your attention from your usual subjects to the problem of the service of general interest, which is so important for european citizens. you have stated, at the end of the consultation on the green paper, that there is general consensus on the need for clarification and legal clarity, as mr langen has just said. but have we reached a consensus on the need for democratic clarity mentioned by mrs flautre? what parliament actually asked for in its resolution - which was not unanimous in reality, we will all agree - is that the interpretation of the court of justice or the commission should not be the only one that prevails in clarifying the concept of acceptable state aid or in defining the correct interpretation of article 86. what is needed is a debate, in the framework of the codecision procedure, which makes it possible to assess the case on a case-by-case basis, since it is true that each person perceives the evidence in the light of his or her historical or national experience. thus, as regards all services of general interest falling within the remit of regional or local authorities, it is clear that the community does not have to intervene. but do they realise that in other countries, both member states and third countries, the evidence could also be in favour of national public services which have worked very well so far? and that, for many citizens too, as regards the effect of liberalisation in areas such as rail transport - for example in a country you know well - or in energy and electricity, it does not seem very obvious that it is absolutely necessary to make the rules of competition the alpha and omega of the organisation. nor does the calculation of state aid and compensation, whether legitimate or not, need to be debated. we therefore believe that a democratic debate must take place. mr langen and his friends very often cite article 86 (3) to prove that this is a matter for the commission, but they fail to cite article 86 (2), which provides that undertakings entrusted with the operation of services of general economic interest are subject to the competition rules in so far as the application of those rules does not prevent the performance, in law or in fact, of the particular task assigned to them. this is something we are discussing among ourselves, but it must also be discussed by the european parliament, the council and the commission, sector by sector.
mr president, to mr langen, i will reply first to this. with your usual vehemence, you are hiding your own failure, because i remind you that you repudiated your own resolution of 2001 in favour of a framework directive, and that you had to accept in january that we repeated our request for a legislative act in codecision. so don't try to hide your failure. mr patten, you are a diplomat and you have a way with words. you said confusion. but where is the confusion when the commission, in its green paper, is totally vague on the fundamental question of funding, and then a few weeks after the end of the debate, it tells us that it will now be holding consultations on funding? democracy which can play a constructive leadership role in the affairs of its region. council. mr president, i welcome the opportunity to brief members of the european parliament today on our plans for the spring european council. the taoiseach, bertie ahern td, wrote to heads of state or government on 17 february 2004 and communicated our proposed priorities for the council, as outlined in the draft annotated agenda for the council, which members will have seen. we intend to reserve the morning session of friday, 26 march for our annual consideration of the lisbon strategy of economic, social and environmental renewal. the parliament will already be aware, from the taoiseach’s address on 14 january 2004, that in its presidency programme, ireland is giving the highest priority to the implementation of the lisbon strategy. as presidency we are acutely conscious that we are almost at the half-way point with regard to the 2010 deadline by which the targets set in 2000 must be reached. it is important to note the considerable progress that has already been achieved on areas ranging from energy liberalisation to the implementation of the internal market in the financial services area. notwithstanding the clear progress that has already been achieved, we must equally recognise that more needs to be done to enable the union to capitalise on the promising signs of economic recovery. we want the european council to convey a message of determination and confidence, demonstrating that the requisite political will exists to enable us to step up the pace of reform. we intend to call on governments, the european parliament and the commission to work together to overcome the obstacles inhibiting the implementation of agreed reforms, so that we can complete the necessary legislative programme and then transpose agreed measures quickly into national law. we have identified two overarching priorities for the spring european council, namely sustainable growth and more and better jobs. we are adopting a holistic approach to the issue of growth, recognising that we need to take action on a range of factors such as competitiveness, innovation, environmental sustainability and social inclusion if we are to make the european economy more dynamic. we need to enhance competitiveness so that our economy can withstand global challenges. it is equally vital that we take specific steps to make the internal market more vibrant. we are focusing, in this regard, on two particular areas: financial services and the services sector more broadly. we believe that an effective single market in the financial services area will enable the eu economy to grow significantly by increasing the provision of more and cheaper capital. we hope that the european parliament can engage constructively with us in pursuing this objective by helping to finalise the remaining elements of the financial services action plan, particularly the proposed directives on transparency and investment services, before the end of its current term. we are all aware that the services sector has powered the eu economy over the past decade, providing a dynamic motor for growth that has accounted for 70% of the eu’s gdp and of its employment opportunities. we see the full application of internal market principles to that sector as a vital tool in enabling competitive businesses to expand throughout the eu and offer greater choice to eu consumers. consequently, we look forward to fruitful cooperation with the parliament in advancing significantly the proposed directive on the internal market for services next year. the lisbon strategy explicitly recognised that for the eu to compete globally, it must make the transition to a knowledge-based economy in which leading-edge technology and expertise will provide crucial added value to eu products and services. however, we continue to lag behind our most important international competitors in terms of our investment in, or the priority attached to, innovation. the number of researchers in the eu accounts for only 5.7 per 1000 workforce, while the corresponding figures are 8.1 per 1000 for the us and 9.1 per 1000 for japan. indeed, as the commission’s spring report has noted, the private sector contributes three times more investment in human capital in japan and a staggering five times more in the us than in the eu. each of our institutions, national governments, the council, the commission and parliament will need to see how we can provide dynamic solutions that will foster a climate in business that is more conducive to innovation. as a first step in that process, we have proposed that the european council should agree that member states should consider targeted supports and incentives to encourage greater research and development investment by businesses. equally, if we are to increase the number of researchers undertaking the work necessary to enable our economy to grow, it is important to look at how we might retain our own researchers and attract researchers from other countries into the eu. the council looks forward, in this regard, to the continued cooperation of parliament to ensure the early adoption of the forthcoming draft directive on the mobility of third country researchers. i am personally committed to the objective of ensuring better regulation within the eu. i firmly believe that better regulation can enable the eu economy to grow significantly by achieving the right balance that will allow the interests of the public to be safeguarded while at the same time easing any unnecessary burdens on business. the presidency has developed a joint initiative with the succeeding presidencies – the netherlands, luxembourg and the uk – aimed at giving priority, over the next two years, to the objective of better regulation. our second priority is that of more and better jobs. our presidency approach to the issue of employment is informed by the recommendations of the employment task force chaired by mr wim kok which reported to the european commission at the end of 2003. we welcome the full incorporation of the task force’s policy messages into the analysis and assessment outlined in the joint employment report. we are proposing, consequently, that the european council should agree that, within an overall employment strategy, member states should give urgent attention to three structural challenges, namely adaptability, greater labour force participation and investment in human capital. as you are aware, we set targets under the lisbon strategy that female labour force participation should reach 60% and that the rate for older workers should increase to 50% by 2010. the commission’s spring report has recorded the increase in the female employment rate over the past three years to 55.6%, in part because of the progress made on improving the availability and accessibility of care facilities for children under three. if we can maintain that rate of progress, we have a realistic chance of meeting the 60% target for female participation by 2010. as presidency, we consider that the most urgent issues needing to be addressed, with regard to attracting more women into the workforce, are the continuing pay disparities experienced by women and the importance of more family-friendly work environments. however, we have more serious difficulties with regard to the target in respect of the employment rate for older workers. the employment rate for the cohort of workers aged between 55 and 64 had reached only 40.1% by 2002, meaning that another 7 million jobs would be required to enable us to meet the 50% target by 2010. conscious of the importance of this issue, the irish presidency is proposing that the right legal and financial incentives be put in place to retain older workers in the workforce. the labour participation issue highlights the reality that implementation of the lisbon strategy requires the commitment not just of national governments but of a range of actors including employers and trade unions. the support of employers is essential, for instance, if we are to create family-friendly and enabling environments that attract and retain female employees and older workers. equally, we need the commitment of trade unions to facilitate the necessary adaptation to change that is increasingly essential in a competitive, global environment. we believe, therefore, that it is essential to explore ways of involving the necessary stakeholders more fundamentally in implementing our lisbon goals. the process of change is unavoidably difficult. however, we can build a better future for the citizens of our union, and of the enlarged union. we believe that the process of implementing the lisbon strategy will benefit greatly from the contribution of the new member states, each of which has had to manage fundamental and wide-ranging economic transformations. while we have much to do, the benefits for our citizens of our implementing the lisbon strategy effectively will be considerable. the prize is a great one. our work programme and the potential benefits for lisbon are well encapsulated in the presidency
