the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking all the members who have contributed to this work and enriched it. since its adoption, the charter of fundamental rights has been the european parliament's reference framework for the preparation of its annual report on fundamental rights, an essential report in our parliamentary life. in fact, the charter of fundamental rights is generally taken as a reading grid. but for 2003, we have opted for a slightly different approach, taking into account only a few articles of the charter that we have confronted with reality and practice. a first question might be asked: why is the european parliament interested in the question of fundamental rights? well, let me remind you that our parliament is the expression of popular sovereignty and therefore it is called upon to decide on matters which directly affect citizens, particularly when their dignity is at stake, since its primary role is to represent them and defend their interests. public freedoms and fundamental rights are enshrined in our constitutions, in our national and european legislation. the draft european constitution even incorporates the charter of fundamental rights in its preamble. the legitimacy of the european parliament in the field of fundamental rights has been strengthened by article 7. on the basis of a reasoned proposal, it may refer the matter to the council where there is a clear risk of a serious breach by a member state of the principles set out in article 6. this report will help to strengthen the european parliament's capacity to carry out its role of monitoring and control of fundamental rights in our union. this is the fourth report. every year, as you know, the report is assigned to a political group. this year, i had the pleasure of doing so. in this report, we have sought to measure the effectiveness of the rights enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights and their effectiveness, which is measured in relation to each individual, regardless of, inter alia, gender, ethnic or cultural origin, sexual orientation, religion, disability or status. we have seen a wealth of measures put in place, especially after 11 september 2001, both at the level of the european union and at the level of the member states, in the field of the fight against terrorism, transnational crime and illegal immigration. today, in the name of the security of the union, limits are being placed on our public freedoms and fundamental rights. many provisions directly or indirectly affect certain vulnerable groups and social movements. the fight against crime, insecurity and terrorism, however legitimate it may be, cannot in any way affect or undermine fundamental rights and democratic freedoms without calling into question the very foundations of our union. on the basis of this observation, we have chosen to prepare this report by focusing on the criminalisation of social movements and vulnerable groups. among the target populations, we have identified, in particular, solidarity and human rights associations, migrants, refugees, victims of human trafficking, roma and gypsies, journalists, women, children, disabled people. three points in particular caught my attention and i shall briefly describe them. as regards freedom of the press, the existence of free and pluralistic media reinforces the principle of democracy. on media pluralism, a report by our colleague, mrs boogerd-quaak, on the risks of violation in the european union, and in particular in italy, has just been put to the vote. i shall not therefore return to this subject, but i will nevertheless recall that this report refers to the information of citizens in the european union, to the obligation of the media and the institutions to respect the right of citizens to be fully and objectively informed. the right to objective information is subject to political manipulation of information. unfortunately, we have seen some examples of this in britain during the war against iraq, and in france during the heatwave. this report shows, for example, that there is a quasi-monopoly exercised by certain authorities and that there is a large concentration in certain countries of television, the private sector or the printed press. freedom of the press is being called into question and often, by this very concentration of the media, the pressure that some journalists are under, depending on their political or ideological affiliation, to give their information is unfortunately once again a challenge to our rights. it will therefore be necessary to amend the directive in order to require member states to preserve media pluralism and to strengthen the protection of the confidentiality of sources. i'm coming to the right of asylum. the right to asylum, which has a humanist tradition in europe, is being replaced by a security policy of closing borders. we have not yet harmonised our laws, we often challenge this right to asylum through different national laws and the treatment and living conditions in detention centres are far from the best. as for the right to health and the possibility for every citizen to have access to this right, we must of course be able to implement them. all these rights are linked to citizenship and we know very well that in today's europe, european citizenship cannot be built without these rights. so i would ask you to be particularly vigilant so that our rights, which are increasingly under threat, remain the only ones governing our policies. finally, in order to be credible, the european union, in order to be able to respect rights itself and to be respected, must sweep up the dust on its doorstep, that is to say, not be afraid to react and sometimes to make amends when certain violations are committed at home.
- mr president, i too share many of the observations and proposals made by my colleague, mrs alima boumediene. i would like to focus briefly on the concerns related to the ultra-security approach which the last european council has just confirmed. aligned with the american model, this positioning is dangerous, fraught with threats and, moreover, overlooks the roots of terrorism. under the guise of combating this scourge, the laws that are being accumulated in each of our countries are already leading to new violations of human rights. i am thinking, for example, of the so-called preventive measures concerning the issuing of visas in germany, of those in the netherlands which allow the near-deportation of 26 000 people, of those in france which have led to an increase of more than one third in expulsions compared with the beginning of 2003. the european approach is moving further and further away from the universal principles of asylum and solidarity. the european union has a long history of supporting the fight against terrorism, and the european union has a long history of supporting terrorism. the same logic prevails in the draft directives aimed at harmonising asylum policy. so, as the un high commissioner for refugees has just said, should we not be concerned about the notion of safe third countries to which refugees could be sent back without any certainty about their safety? finally, the same logic applies to the european charters, which our parliament has fortunately just rejected. on the contrary, the future of human rights in europe depends on a genuine policy of welcoming, equal rights - including the right for everyone to vote and be elected in all elections - and also full respect for freedom of expression, including trade union freedoms.
council. mr president, this is an interesting debate, because we are discussing a report of the world bank. the extractive industries review launched by the world bank group in 2001 will guide the bank’s involvement in the oil, gas and mining sectors. the consultative process is a significant element of the group’s overall review of its activities in this area. it is important to note that the result of this initiative – in the form of the comprehensive consultation report produced by the review team, led by dr salim – is being examined by the world bank, and its response to that review is awaited. so in a sense, we are discussing something that is a work in progress. the process must be allowed to take its course in view of the significant recommendations in the review. the importance of protecting and managing the resource base of economic and social development was reaffirmed by heads of state and government at the world summit on sustainable development in johannesburg in september 2002. raw materials, such as minerals and petroleum, provide the foundations for economic growth and well-being, both in industry and in our everyday lives. they are essential in manufacturing, transport, heating and other activities and, most important of all, they are essential in the countries in which the extractive activity takes place. while mineral extraction makes a substantial contribution to economic development, the benefits must be balanced by measures to foster the environmental and social pillars of sustainable development through good governance. this is the area most members will probably be concerned about, because good governance has not always been present. in recognition of the need to balance these demands, actions were agreed in relation to managing the natural resource base in a sustainable and integrated manner. the world bank is not alone in recognising the need to address all elements of sustainable development. in many ways this review parallels work carried out by the european union in recent years, such as strengthening the governance of mining through, for example, amendment of the seveso directive and a proposed new directive on the management of extractive industry waste – an issue that is of concern right across the union. the european union is also taking forward policy on sustainable development through initiatives such as the planned thematic strategy on sustainable use of natural resources. at its meeting on 2 march, the council of environment ministers gave broad policy orientations in relation to the future development of the thematic strategy. the extractive industry review recognises the potential contribution of mining and petroleum to the world bank’s primary mandate – i.e. the alleviation of poverty – and proposes a considerable number of measures in this regard. they merit some detailed consideration. i note also that the world bank has endorsed the transparency initiative launched at the johannesburg summit. this is a particularly important initiative. this, again, is a complex issue and there is a need for greater clarity on how taxes and royalties for such operations are distributed. i should also say that there is probably a need to consider whether they are properly or appropriately distributed – but that is for another time. detailed environmental protection measures in the extractive industries review include proposals such as closure planning and guidelines on tailings management in extractive industries. in many ways these reflect concerns that we are also addressing. the european union guidance note on best available techniques for mining wastes is very advanced and will set out best practice in this area. many local factors, such as climatic conditions, determine the most appropriate ways to mitigate potential adverse impacts. nevertheless, our work in europe will make a useful contribution to better environmental practice and standards in managing mining waste, as well as the cyanide code of practice developed by the unep through multi-stakeholder consultation and participation. we support the conclusions of the johannesburg summit and the plan of implementation, including the specific commitments in relation to the mining, minerals, metals and energy sectors. we also support the promotion of corporate responsibility and accountability, and the exchange of best practices in the context of sustainable development. our position on these issues is clear and, i expect, well known to all interests, including the world bank. nonetheless, our interests and concerns in those areas are worth underlining and restating. climate change remains one of the most significant environmental concerns for the union. the union remains fully committed, for example, to delivering on the kyoto protocol target. as parties to the united nations framework convention on climate change and ratifiers of the kyoto protocol, the european community and its member states are eager to ensure that the activities of the world bank are in harmony with the european union’s objective of stabilising greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere at safe levels. according to the report of the intergovernmental panel on climate change, global emissions of greenhouse gases will need to be drastically cut over the rest of this century if this goal is to be achieved. the recommendations of the extractive industries review in this regard are consistent with a recognised need to move to less carbon-intensive sources of energy. the promotion of cleaner and less greenhouse-gas-emitting energy sources in developing countries, with a particular focus on the promotion of renewable sources of energy, are in keeping with meeting the objectives of the eu’s long-term climate change objectives. in conclusion, we look forward to the response of the world bank to this review. as i said, the response is still forthcoming. we welcome the wide-ranging and transparent nature of the consultation involved in this process and appreciate that the work now under way by the bank is well informed by dr salim's report. the european union’s progressive approach to sustainable development is well known, and we also anticipate a response from the world bank that will be consistent with its overall mission, in particular in poverty reduction and the promotion of sustainable development.
commission. mr president, the extractive industries review, commissioned by the world bank, is an important report and its recommendations should be carefully examined by the european investment bank, the european bank for reconstruction and development and the commission. the commission is a grant donor focusing on poverty alleviation. extractive industry support within the european community development programme has virtually ceased. the specific instrument in the mining sector, sysmin, was discontinued under the cotonou agreement. under the ninth european development fund, any programmes in the mining sector have been defined by partner countries themselves, in line with the ownership concept. less than six percent of funds have been allocated to mining activities in national indicative programmes. in addition, increasing environmental concerns within the european union have led to the generalisation of the use of environmental impact assessments since the 1990s. this also applies to cooperation with financial institutions such as the european investment bank or the world bank. the oecd discusses guidelines for officially supported export credits. it recently announced an agreement to strengthen common approaches for evaluating the environmental impact of infrastructure projects supported by the export credit agencies of oecd governments to ensure that they meet established international standards. as parliament is aware, the european union launched an 'eu energy initiative for poverty eradication and sustainable development' at the world summit on sustainable development in johannesburg in september 2002. the initiative’s secretariat is housed within the commission. it aims to respond to the very issues raised by parliament, by contributing to providing the access to energy necessary for the achievement of the millennium development goals. this objective will be achieved within the context of activities driven by participating developing countries, through the provision of adequate, affordable, sustainable energy services. although the initiative does not have a technology focus, it strives to promote the provision of affordable and sustainable energy services. in doing so, it seeks to promote the choice of the most economic solutions on the basis of economic, social and environmental impacts. this involves the promotion of cleaner and more efficient fossil fuel technologies. the commission also houses the secretariat of the johannesburg renewable energy coalition. this coalition aims to enhance renewable energy deployment within developing countries. let me conclude by assuring you that the commission supports the call for the full implementation of the recommendations of the extractive industries review, which relate to the sustainability of investments, the promotion of good governance, popular consent, social and environmental impact assessment and the respect of human rights and core labour standards.
- mr president, after the un report on the situation in the congo and the us government report on global warming, it is now a report commissioned by the world bank itself that confirms the fears long expressed by the greens. the world bank has set up a study on extractive industries, which, after two years of consultation with civil society, governments and businesses, has delivered a damning report for its development policy. the report highlights the shortcomings and counterproductive effects of the world bank's policy in resource-rich countries. in the study's own words, the world bank has thus attracted too many investors, without really being interested in helping countries develop their capacity to turn their natural wealth into means of fighting poverty. the commission also points out the shortcomings of the world bank's environmental and social surveillance activities. the study argues that if the full force of the market is unleashed in the absence of robust frameworks, the damage can be particularly severe. there are many examples of odious financing. the yanacocha gold mine in peru is the prototype of the toxic tragedy. the mine, operated by an american company, flattened five mountains, displaced thousands of people and caused cyanide pollution of water throughout the region. the world bank also supported the chad-cameroon oil pipeline, which we were the only ones to fight and which had disastrous social and environmental consequences: mass migration, increased food insecurity, increased prostitution leading to the spread of aids. can we really talk about development policy? the exploitation of oil, gas or mining does not necessarily mean poverty reduction. in countries where corruption is still high, legal frameworks are unreliable and democratic practices are uncertain, the world bank is unfortunately not doing anything to promote sustainable development. on the contrary, in many countries, the extractive industries have been linked to human rights violations and civil strife, as was seen in burma. worse, more than 80% of the world bank's oil financing actually feeds the north and not the poor countries. as a result of this blind liberal investment, countries with disappointing results outperform countries with substantial progress. the greens, in line with the study's recommendations, advocate the cessation of financing for oil projects by 2008, the cessation of financing for coal mines to combat greenhouse gases, the promotion of clean and renewable energy and energy efficiency. the european union has a major role to play here by calling, through its member states, for the world bank to take account of the study's recommendations. the world bank has been on the wrong track for too long, and it is time for a change of direction so that development policy can finally benefit those most in need. - the next item is the report (a5-0060/2004) by mr miguélez ramos, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation on the conclusion of the protocol amending the fourth protocol on the conditions governing fishing provided for in the agreement on fisheries between the european economic community, on the one hand, and the government of denmark and the home rule government of greenland, on the other (com (2003) 609 - c5-0514/2003 - 2003/0236 (cns)).
commission. madam president, i wish to begin by making it clear that i have inherited my knowledge on this subject from my colleague, mr fischler, who, unfortunately, cannot be here today. however, i will gladly take on board what has been said and try to address as far as possible the arguments put forward in this debate. firstly, i shall try to clarify the commission's position concerning the amendments that have been tabled. first of all on amendment no 1: the financial compensation of the agreement is one single compensation, which corresponds to access to the waters, as well as compensation for the impact caused by the activity of european union vessels in third-country waters. the fact that the third country in the framework of a fisheries sector dialogue accepts to commit a part of the financial compensation to activities in support of a reform of its own fisheries policy, does not constitute an argument for a differentiation in two different financial envelopes. the approach of differentiating financial compensation would result in the refusal of the third country to commit itself to reform its fisheries policy. therefore the commission cannot accept amendment no 1. on amendment no 2, which, to a certain extent – if i have understood you correctly – is connected with amendment no 5, considering the fact that the commission is responsible for the sound financial management of the community funds, amendment no 2 cannot be accepted. indeed, the budgetary authority must give the commission the means and the legal basis to ensure the sound financial management of this agreement. despite some transfers made in 2003 by the quota-holding member states, experience shows that these have not been sufficient to ensure the optimum utilisation of the fishing possibilities and thus sound financial management. with respect to the argument put forward, how can we guarantee that the principle of relative stability and article 20(5) of the basic regulation are adhered to? i would like to underline that the temporary transfer of fishing possibilities from one member state to another by the commission is not contrary to the principle of relative stability, because, in accordance with article 20(1) of council regulation (ec) no 2371/2002 on the allocation of fishing possibilities among member states, such a transfer will not have an effect on the allocation of fishing possibilities between the member states in greenland waters in the future. the allocation continues – and will continue – to be ruled, on the basis of the distribution keys, as before. the member states that benefit from a temporary transfer cannot exploit the catches made for the changing of the basis of the allocation for the future. the determination of the fishing possibilities is made on the basis of scientific reports. one innovation of this agreement is precisely that all quotas are now subject to an annual revision, if scientific advice so requests. also, i cannot accept the idea that with this mechanism we are creating a precedent. the transfer clause exists and is implemented in all other third-country agreements with financial compensation, without any problem. the only agreement that does not have this kind of article is precisely the greenland agreement. that is the situation we want to change now. i want to say that in 2003 the commercial value of the catches, including the real catches of the transfers made to norway, iceland and the faroes amounted to eur 50 million. compared to the current financial compensation of eur 42.82 million, this is not satisfactory. in an agreement with financial compensation, it is unacceptable that the commission does not have the means to ensure that community funds are not wasted. having said that, the commission welcomes the last amendment – amendment no 5. we are responsible for ensuring the sound financial management of community funds. amendment no 5 shows the willingness of the budgetary authority to provide the commission with the legal basis to ensure such a ground management without prejudice to relative stability, as i have said before. on amendment no 3, we agree with the spirit thereof, but we believe that the commission already complies with the transmission of this kind of information in line with both the current interinstitutional arrangements and, in particular, with the framework agreement between the commission and the european parliament. therefore, amendment no 3 is not necessary. finally, we cannot accept amendment no 4. i recall in this respect the established principle regarding the nature of a protocol to a fisheries agreement. in light of the fact that this is an annex to the framework agreement, its periodic renewal does not require a new mandate.

- the next item is the report (a5-0211/2004) by mr ingo schmitt, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the initiative of the kingdom of spain on the draft council directive on the obligation of carriers to provide passenger data (6620/2004 - c5-0111/2004 - 2003/0809 (cns)).
- madam president, in an increasingly complex context of managing migration flows and combating illegal immigration, it is very difficult for us to accept this spanish initiative, both in substance and form. in formal terms, to accept this initiative would be to endorse the council's working method of constantly amending texts proposed to parliament. i commend the rapporteur's work and his excellent consistency. the commission received new versions of the report after it had already drawn up its report, the previous text having become obsolete. this is unacceptable. we are appalled by this lack of coordination in the council and by this disregard for parliament and the representatives of the peoples of europe, not to mention the energy and time wasted as a result. then we can ask ourselves what the result was. is it really effective? the last official text of the spanish initiative contains the words 'obligation' and 'sanction' in almost every paragraph. the objective is clearly defined, namely to combat illegal immigration. the sanctions should therefore primarily concern smugglers. well, no, you won't. sanctions and obligations apply to airlines and we cannot accept that states abdicate their responsibilities, thus offloading the burden on private companies and then sanctioning them if the work is done poorly. requiring private airlines to collect data to control illegal immigration is tantamount to requiring carriers to assume the obligations of states. the objective of reducing illegal immigration is right, but how effective can the proposed text be? the real operational usefulness of this text has not been demonstrated. the fact that only air carriers are concerned already weakens the objective of this directive. this text, if accepted as it stands, would completely disrupt the work of airlines, since the transmission of data, which is compulsory for these companies, represents a considerable burden in terms of costs. in some countries passports cannot be read by machines, in others this type of machine is not yet available: to remedy these shortcomings member states do not provide for any compensation system. in addition, the system of penalties would be extremely burdensome and would not take account of the efforts made by the companies which have been convicted to meet these obligations. in conclusion, while illegal immigration must be combated, there are, in my view, many other ways. we therefore reject this initiative and would like the commission to make a proposal in the future, a coherent proposal which respects the competences and the rights and duties of citizens. we trust the commission to make this happen.

mr president, the marinho report on asylum systems in europe seems to me to be missing the point. what was the question? the first and foremost question was how to respond to the report presented by the uk government to the european council last spring, entitled 'new international approaches to the processing of asylum and protection applications'. this report, which was very sensible, raised the broad question of the need to take back control of asylum systems which are currently being perverted under the pressure of immense migratory flows. it was followed by a commission communication which makes simple issues complex and drowns the fish under the title 'towards more accessible, fair and organised asylum systems', a title which completely misrepresents the british report. it is remarkable that the european parliament's report under consideration today draws heavily on the commission's communication, but does not even mention the uk government's report in its references. such contempt for a member state is hardly tolerable to me. i shall therefore be relying on this report. it makes four findings: one, financial aid to refugees is poorly distributed; second, the current asylum regime fails to benefit the vast majority of the most vulnerable refugees, who remain in place with little protection. third, the vast majority of asylum seekers in the european union do not meet the criteria for refugee status or subsidiary protection; fourthly, the majority of those denied asylum are staying in our country illegally and are not being sent back to their countries of origin. in the face of these challenges, the uk report calls for the creation of protection zones in regions of origin to provide accessible shelters and for the establishment of transit processing centres outside the union from which admitted refugees could be offered access to participating countries and others returned to their countries of origin. the report before us today only gives a few examples of these questions and proposals. in particular, it rejects the idea of protection zones or transit centres outside the union, because they would not be sufficiently protective (see paragraph 16), and it proposes, in order to deal with the increase in false asylum applications, to widen the possibilities for legal immigration - as mr marinho has just reminded us (see paragraph 8), which would in fact be a remedy far worse than the evil. overall, mr president, this report does not seem to have taken account of the dramatic problem facing our societies, which are now struggling to survive, or of the need to revise our asylum procedures in depth and to focus our efforts primarily on political stabilization and economic development in the countries where this emigration of despair is taking place.
mr president, the intergovernmental fund for financing cooperation between the european union and the acp countries, known as the edf, which has a five-year duration under the cotonou agreements, has been operating since 1959 on the basis of contributions from the states, with costs being shared. france and germany now provide almost 42% of the total funding. the funds are managed by the commission with delegation to the beneficiary countries. for the period 2003-07, more than €15 billion is available for new commitments and more than €10 billion for payments. it is scandalous that 11 billion euros of surplus funds are available because they have not been used under the 6th, 7th and 8th edfs. after many unsuccessful attempts by the commission, it thought that with the 9th edf expiring in 2007, the enlargement of the union being a given, and the debate on the financial framework after 2006 having been launched, it was appropriate to discuss again the budgetisation of the edf. the commission thus joined the constant concern expressed for years by parliament, which is concerned about budgetary discipline, the prompt and efficient use of resources and the co-decision role which would be conferred on it by budgeting, whereas today its role in this area is non-existent and it simply cannot fulfil its budgetary control task. in the face of current dysfunctions, what are the advantages of budgeting? first, to give democratic legitimacy through parliamentary control over the financing of the edf. secondly, to put an end to the burdens of procedures, to streamline and simplify them, to bring them closer to the beneficiaries, to speed up the disbursement of funds and to improve the efficiency of aid. thirdly, to introduce transparency. the complexity of the current system makes it totally opaque in terms of the use of funds. fourthly, as regards the balance to be cleared, namely the 11 billion euros i mentioned earlier, budgeting could bring about considerable improvements. fifth, to ensure the contribution of all states. as you know, if the edf remains outside the budget, the overall value of the 10th edf may be limited by the small contribution of the 10 new members of the european union. on the other hand, if the edf is budgeted, the contributions of the member states will be fixed by budgetary rules. sixthly, to avoid delays in the entry into force of the edf due to the obligation of the member states and the acp countries to ratify the cotonou financial protocol. if the edf is budgeted, ratification disappears, thus saving time in the use of edf funds. of course there are risks and the acp countries, like some of the member states of the union, are particularly sensitive to these risks. the risks are: ensuring a fixed level of funding, fearing that funds earmarked for acp countries will be used for other purposes or transferred to other uses, as was the case for iraq or afghanistan, as might be the case for the reconstruction of a state. this concern is real and it is clear that the budget has the technical means to preserve the appropriations allocated to the edf. the financial perspective sets ceilings for the headings for several years and therefore it would be sufficient to create a sub-heading, as is the case today for headings 1 and 7, in order to avoid and limit this risk. secondly, there is the whole problem of multiannual programming. the edf covers five years. over five years, these funds can be used, carried forward. the acp countries fear that, in the context of budgeting, unused funds will be lost after one year. we therefore ask, with the commission's agreement, for a regulation to be drawn up which will establish the multiannual nature of the edf and allow the funds to be used in accordance with technical criteria which will have to be put in place and which already exist practically today. this is important because it would reassure the acp countries, who are afraid not only of a reduction in the overall amount of the edf but also of losing a large part of the funds previously allocated to them. secondly, and this is important psychologically, humanly, politically and technically, the acp countries must be involved in the management of these european development funds. how did you do that? we propose this in article 11: simply by giving the acp parliamentary assembly and the acp countries the capacity to question, the capacity to verify, the capacity to protest against the use of these funds, which would be done under the control of the european parliament and in co-decision with the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, these are the points i wanted to make very quickly. everyone knows about this file. if it were to be voted on tomorrow and if, in the future, it were to receive the approval of the member states - which will be a difficult task, as will also the approval of the acp countries - it would be a real revolution, because we would finally see the third policy of the union which was not budgeted fall within the framework of the budget of the european union, which seems to us to be a plus for us, for the acp countries and above all for the development policy which is in great need of it.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, the report by mr scarbonchi raises a number of good questions. for several years now, we greens have been fighting for parliamentary control and transparency, which are the hallmarks of democracy. it is normal that the allocation and use of appropriations should be controlled by a representative and democratic body. it is true that the edf has not yet exhibited these characteristics. budgeting is one way of ensuring control of this programme. it does, however, bring new problems. how can we avoid the risk of transferring funds from one budget line to another if we do not provide for a form of sanctuarization? how can we prevent the development of large projects favouring powerful states from being preferred to initiatives by less influential states or to micro-projects which are closer to the needs of the population? - mr president, we have opposed the forthcoming enlargement of the european union to ten new member states. this was not a position of principle, but my group and i, the french edd delegation, have expressed our opposition to an unrealistic integration timetable and to the accession of countries which, like us, are not close to such a leap into the unknown. our position on turkey's membership is quite different. we are opposed to this on a matter of principle. as general de gaulle said, the facts are stubborn. geographically, historically and culturally, turkey is not a european country. however, as stated in article 49 of the treaty on european union, the candidate countries must be european countries. i shall only mention two additional arguments among the many already mentioned. first, in the multipolar world in which we live, turkey is an eastern power; it plays a leading role among the turkic-speaking peoples of central asia, it shares long borders with iran, iraq and syria and we do not think that the european union has a place in such an unstable region. secondly, the political representation of countries in the european union is linked to their demographic weight. turkey will eventually be more populated than any european state. we do not want a country whose accession is so controversial to become a political heavyweight of the european union. after years of hesitation on the opening of negotiations on turkey's accession, the vote on this report is an opportunity to send a strong political signal. although we share the many criticisms of turkey's lack of preparation, we will vote against a report which sets out turkey's progress towards membership, because we, like many of our fellow citizens, are opposed to membership. secondly, and finally, i would like to ask a question: where will the expansion of this so-called european union end?

commission. mr president, this is the third time that i have come to a plenary session to address the issue of payments. an efficient and secure payment system is an essential complement to the free movement of goods and services in the european union. let me give you one figure to illustrate this. every eu citizen carries out, on average, 138 non-cash payment transactions each year. an efficient system must be based on a robust and dynamic regulatory framework that ensures competition, consumer protection and safety in payment transactions. pan-european trade needs an effective underlying payment system if it is to expand. the regulation on cross-border payments adopted in 2001 has made it easier and cheaper to perform many types of payments in euro within the internal market. however, we are not yet where we want to be and need to be. significant obstacles remain, as are highlighted in our communication. to deliver an improved regulatory environment for payments, remaining legal and technical barriers to intra-eu payments should be identified and removed. in other words, the whole internal market ought to be transformed into one efficient domestic payment area. that is our main purpose. eu legislation in this field is necessary. but for certain issues, self- or co-regulation could be the best approach. that also satisfies mr radwan's desire for more subsidiarity. as always, the solution should be proportionate to the problem it is intended to solve. the four guiding principles for the commission’s future regulatory proposal should be as follows. firstly, to modernise the existing eu legislation on payments. secondly, to inject more competition into this market for the ultimate benefit of our citizens. the basic idea is that the provision of payment services should be open to all appropriate providers, but without sacrificing consumer protection. we must therefore design an appropriate supervisory framework matching all types of payment service providers. the guiding principle here must be: 'same business, same risks, same rules'. thirdly, we need to develop a trustworthy pan-european payment area in which consumers feel that they have the same protection, no matter where they are and what kind of payment instrument they use. a single and balanced set of rules should be defined on parties' rights and obligations regarding, for example, misuse of a payment instrument and revocability of payment orders. fourthly, we need to incorporate the relevant financial action task force, or fatf, special recommendations into eu legislation to combat the financing of criminal activities. let me stress that given their decisive contribution to the competitiveness of our economy, payments are high on the commission’s agenda. we shall need the strong support of this parliament, and in this respect i am encouraged by the terms of the resolution which has been put forward by mr radwan. i welcome all amendments submitted by members of this house. i shall wind up by thanking mr radwan for the report which he has submitted and i assure him that, just as he wishes to have less bureaucracy, that is precisely what this commissioner and the commission as a whole also want.
- mr president, it is a pity that the debate on consumer credit and the debate on the single payment area have not been joined because they have a common issue: do we want to build a european market for retail financial services? priority has so far been given to wholesale and investment services. the only notable but important initiative during this parliamentary term was the regulation on the pricing of crossborder payment transactions in the euro area. so this debate is important and i think we need to now set a clear political objective; i think that is what the commission wants. the euro can only become a real asset if the euro area is built as a domestic space for means of payment. to achieve this, it is absolutely necessary to achieve interbank infrastructure. the payment service activity does require the removal of national obstacles, but at the same time it requires prudential supervision. it is on this basis that the internal market for retail banking, and in particular consumer credit, will be able to develop, allowing the emergence of european banking players. of course, in this integrated space, account will have to be taken of the diversity of operators, and in particular of the specificities of savings banks and mutual funds. but what is the right method to move forward? the application of the country of origin rule with minimum harmonisation seems to us to be negative, both from the point of view of consumer protection and fair competition. mr radwan's report, which is leaning in this direction, gives far too much credit to self-regulation. however, on the other hand, maximum harmonisation would leave no room for diversity and would also be problematic. that is why i think the right solution is to agree on common principles of general interest, common concepts, in particular for access by all to payment methods with a high level of security, low-cost services but in which there is a high level of trust. the rules for cross-border operations must be precise and strong cooperation between national regulators is necessary. in this context, i think that several points in mr radwan's report call for adjustments. the commission has proposed that the maximum amount of liability for a transaction which the customer has not authorised be reduced to € 150 before the customer is challenged. in the case of a pan-european direct debit, the debtor must be able to refuse a direct debit before it is made to his bank. in the event of a substantial change in the rate, the closure or transfer of the account must be carried out free of charge at the request of the customer. it is also necessary to restore the responsibility of providers throughout the payment chain. on the other hand, a stronger community regulation is needed to combat the financing of terrorism. the full information regime should therefore apply to both extra-community and intra-community transfers.

vice-president of the commission. (es) madam president, on the question of the legal basis, i repeat what i said earlier. i shall therefore concentrate on the various speeches and amendments to mr seppänen's report. first of all, i would like to thank you for the debate on a very important subject and for the quality of the 43 amendments, which does not mean that we can accept all of them. and i would like to thank the rapporteur in particular for the excellent work he has done and also mr mombaur, who has left the house, although i do not agree with his approach to changing the legal basis, but he has also worked in a very constructive way. i should like to point out that the commission cannot support amendments which restrict the scope of the draft regulation to cross-border trade only. that would in some ways greatly reduce the scope and the aim of this proposal. we could trade gas from one country to another without problems, but we would clearly restrict internal competition. in several states - including some of the new ones - gas is transported through several networks, some of which are not connected to an import point and therefore not to a cross-border point either. all such transport networks and the undertakings concerned would be excluded from the scope of the proposed regulation, which would seriously impede and undermine the proper functioning of the internal market. but the scope of application is also that laid down in the transit directive and the second directive on the internal gas market. we are talking about facilitating competition not only between countries but within countries. restricting the scope of this regulation would severely limit the objective and the possibilities of genuinely achieving a competitive european gas market. but it should also be noted that some people - mr mombaur in particular - have raised the need to ensure a certain return on investment which would make it attractive to spend money on the construction, commissioning and maintenance of gas networks. in this connection i should like to say that we can accept amendment no 12, which we believe clarifies and improves the quality of our text, which takes account of competition between different networks - which was not explicitly covered in our text - and which we therefore believe can put an end to the fears that some had about the lack of profitability and, therefore, the future problems for new investments. i would point out that the minimum standards on access conditions to transport networks are absolutely key. without these conditions it is clear that the entry of new competitors would in fact be prevented and, therefore, the realisation of the genuine gas market would be 'impeded'. another question raised was that of the madrid forum, and whether we should go a little further in some respects - which is one of the approaches - and, above all, in the future, whether we should forget the forum by means of the comitology procedure or forget the sector, the protagonists in the sector. i want to make it clear, as the honourable members know, that over the years i have insisted on the need to listen to the main players in a systematic way and we are therefore prepared to consider a solution which ensures that the sector - in addition to the stakeholders - is consulted in the madrid forum. amendment no 3 could provide a possible solution in this respect. in any case, we do not want to exclude the sector, but on the contrary to keep it always included and, looking to the future, we intend to support the madrid forum. the commission, while not intending to go beyond the madrid forum's proposals, does believe that one of the proposals made by eurogas to the madrid forum, relating to the use it or loose it principle, is essential in the field of contracts. otherwise, through a priori contracts, actual access to third parties could be clearly blocked and competition thus restricted. in this sense, future use contracts must also be based on the use it or loose it principle, the only way to ensure that they are real contracts and not contracts whose sole purpose is to use or saturate the available capacities and thus create artificial congestion on the networks which would prevent access by third parties. it must be said that amendments which clarify or support the provisions of the draft regulation, which is in general in line with the guidelines of the madrid forum - as has been pointed out and acknowledged by the honourable members - can be accepted, at least in part or if its wording is changed. this is the case with amendments nos 1 and 22, and many others which i will not mention. for this purpose we shall give the detailed enumeration. as regards certain technical matters - commission. mr president, as my colleague mr fischler stated yesterday, the commission took immediate action when it had evidence of the problems in eurostat. this has resulted in a thorough restructuring of the eurostat directorate-general and its operations. in addition to the statement made by my colleague on behalf of the commission, i would like to emphasise the measures regarding in particular the revision of the code of conduct, the improvement of the flow of information related to fraud allegations, as well as a revision of the legal framework of olaf. i would particularly like to point out the following measures. firstly, revising the code of conduct that governs relations between the commissioners and their services and which emphasises the political responsibility of the commissioner, as well as that of the director-general or the head of service. the new code includes specific procedures requiring the commissioner to be informed about any fact, situation or question concerning management – especially financial management – the gravity of which could invoke the responsibility of the commissioner or the college. secondly, putting in place measures aimed at facilitating the cross-referencing of any information related to fraud allegations, helping to ensure that the political level is kept informed and that any cases detected are properly followed up. thirdly, strengthening information circuits between the central services and operational services, especially in the areas of control and internal audit. this involves a series of important measures that aim at fine-tuning financial management reforms that had already been introduced by the prodi commission. these measures derive essentially from the recommendations which the internal auditor made in his report on dg eurostat's contracts - informing and training staff about the different mechanisms in place for whistleblowing and revising olaf's legal framework with the adoption of two new legislative proposals to be examined by the new parliament. these proposals aim to improve the information flows within the institutions of the union and to reinforce the procedural guarantees. despite the crisis, eurostat's functions in performing the essential statistical work of the commission have not been interrupted. a major reorganisation of eurostat was approved by the commission on 29 september 2003 and the new establishment plan has been in operation since 1 november. the system of approval for commitments and payments was reorganised. the financial circuits were more explicitly defined so as to bring into play the responsibilities of the delegated authorising officers at head of unit and directorate level. the commission's decision to end the contractual links with four companies required a significant amount of work in ending the contracts themselves and in ensuring that the potential for litigation was minimised. following on from the special audit undertaken by the internal audit service in september 2003, as well from the in-depth audit that had recently been concluded, a series of initiatives generated by the annual activity report were also undertaken. there will be a radical new departure in the field of providing statistical information. based on the principle that european statistical information is a public service, all statistical data drawn up and collected by eurostat should be available free of charge to users and should be available on the internet. finally, the work programme for 2004 is strictly prioritised and intentionally realistic. the emphasis is on the essential missions of eurostat, namely the production of figures and independent statistics. the commission is keen to reduce its dependence on external companies and organisations and to ensure that the european statistical service remains a public service which is open and available to users and acts in the public interest. the commission has thus taken very concrete and swift measures to respond to the criticism made by the european parliament in its resolution of 17 december 2003 on the commission's legislative and work programme for 2004. this is also confirmed in the commission's progress report of 9 february 2004 on completing the reform mandate. the commission would like to thank the european parliament and the rapporteur, mr bayona de perogordo, for having voted today by a large majority to grant discharge to the commission in respect of the execution of the general budget of the european communities for 2002. this vote confirms that the eurostat affair is a very regrettable exception to the generally sound financial management of the budget of the european communities. however, the eurostat affair also shows the necessity and the importance of the reform progress engaged by the commission. with regard to the political responsibility mentioned in the motion of censure that is going to be debated here tonight, i would from recurring, and that the commission has learned its lesson with regard to the problem of inadequate information flows revealed by the eurostat case and has taken appropriate action. president profession, including employee organisations, will be present on the agency's board of directors. they will also have the opportunity to participate in working groups on the tsis which concern them. openness and liberalization. the unbridled race for ever more liberalisation is one of the sources of discontent with europe. with the directive on the opening of networks, total freight liberalisation is proposed, even though the first package has just been transposed and no serious, transparent and contradictory assessment of its effects has been carried out. moreover, a date for the full liberalisation of passenger transport has been announced, pre-empting the debate which has not yet begun on the third package. i think we must stop ignoring the opposition voiced by all the railway workers' unions in europe. so, even on a subject as important and decisive as safety, we are being asked to amend article 1 to bring openness to competition and safety on the same level. i think we are sending the wrong message. i do not want to repeat here - as my colleagues know - what i have already said on this subject on several occasions. i would simply say that on matters of this importance, with the experience we have in europe, we would benefit from adopting the precautionary principle.
the rapporteur. - mr president, madam commissioner, i should like to begin by thanking all my colleagues, first of all the rapporteurs of these four important reports, but also all the colleagues in creates mechanisms that will soon be unmanageable, especially when we want to push enlargement a little further, towards the balkans and perhaps beyond. i therefore hope that the commitment made by sustainable mobility, that is to say, the development of railways and waterways, rather than succumbing to the inflation of cars, which will one day pose us with serious political problems. i believe that openness, in the sense in which we conceive it, that is to say, purely liberal openness, competition on the networks is not the panacea. today, however, we are working blindly towards that goal. in reality, we know very well that interoperability is not financed. we are well aware that there are enormous investments to be made and that the financial perspectives do not meet the demand for financial resources expressed by commissioner de palacio herself to finance the transeuropean transport networks and, in particular, the railway networks. i mean, i don't think anything's going to happen. today it is a step forward without the railway workers, because there are national cultures - that's how it is - extremely strong in these companies which are labour-intensive companies. i think that sectoral dialogue should be given priority before guidelines are adopted, and that is what we have done this time. we must continue along this path, but i also hope that we will one day move towards a collective agreement for railway workers, whether they are employed by private companies or by public companies, so that they themselves can take up this great renaissance of rail, which is of general interest to all those who aspire to a less polluting mode of transport.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr rübig, for his excellent work, which will enable us to adopt this proposal at first reading. it is a good example of effective and constructive cooperation between the institutions. the commission proposal has two main components. it provides for the closure of the joint european venture programme and makes some changes to the european mechanism for supporting start-up capital for technology companies, the so-called start up etf. this facility provides venture capital for the launch of technology companies. the proposed closure of the jev programme is the result of an evaluation of the programme which concluded that it had not achieved its objectives. demand has been low and the impact on job creation limited. i think this proposal sends a clear message that both parliament and the commission are prepared to close ineffective programmes that do not achieve their objectives. it is preferable for the commission to devote its financial and human resources to financial instruments for smes that have a greater impact, such as the sme guarantee facility and the european etf start up start-up capital support facility. as regards the proposed changes to this support mechanism, they will allow it to become a flexible instrument. these changes will improve the availability of seed capital funding for companies up to ten years old, compared to five years at present, if they are active in particular sectors such as life sciences. this reflects the fact that product development and the experimental phase can be particularly long for these companies and that, during this time, they need access to risk capital in order to continue their activities. the commission proposal also makes a more explicit reference to the eligibility of investment funds in companies carrying out research and development activities. this helps to underline that the european support mechanism for start-up capital is open to funds which are dedicated to small and medium-sized enterprises particularly active in research and development. i conclude by saying that these changes to the start-up capital support mechanism should help to achieve both the lisbon objectives and the 3% of gdp target for research and development expenditure. i am therefore pleased to see that the rapporteur. - mr president, i am very pleased that the commission has taken this decision. as you are no doubt aware, the objective is to make the european union the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustainable economic growth, accompanied by a quantitative and qualitative improvement in employment and greater social cohesion. europe - let us not forget - has already made a number of considerable progresses, since we have created six million jobs on the european continent since 1999. however, it is clear that despite this progress, europe will not reach the intermediate quantitative target of 67% employment by 2005. today, a major french newspaper headlined 'europe in a growth freeze', a growth which will be only 1.7%. that is why, in the face of this slowdown in the economy, we must do everything we can and the european union must react. it is in this context that mr wim kok's report was produced. the report stressed the urgent need for concrete action by taking decisive action in the areas of taxation, social affairs, the environment, research and innovation, in all areas, including job creation, while taking account of globalisation and the ageing population. this requires a large degree of rapid reaction and good change management. that's why we must choose change to avoid it. this is why i wanted to emphasise in my report the practical implementation of the employment guidelines. first, the responsiveness of enterprises and their employees must be improved. this requires adaptation through increased levels of human capital and a lifelong learning policy which must be encouraged. this also requires measures to encourage the creation of enterprises, especially small enterprises. it is in this spirit - and this is the subject of amendment 7 to the report - that europe must support networks and partnerships, for example platforms of excellence which bring together small businesses, research centres, universities and private companies. secondly, the labour force and the entire population must be mobilised. in this spirit, i am advocating - and this is the subject of amendment no 5 - that youth employment should be made a major european cause. thirdly, a comprehensive european plan against deindustrialisation must be launched. in this spirit - and this is the subject of amendment no 6 - it is certainly important that the european union should support the most disadvantaged regions without neglecting to support the development of the most dynamic territories. this is the subject of amendment no 5. fourthly, the very concrete approach to better governance. this is the conclusion of the wim kok report. better governance means the need to mobilise all actors - national parliaments, regional and local actors, social partners, trade unions, associations and businesses - and to facilitate, in this spirit, better access to the structural funds. until now, europe has supported the policy of the member states but in a spirit of assistance, adopting a policy - i would like to say - of assistance by means of crutches, but not in a spirit of economic dynamism. i think that while we must bear in mind the need to support the most disadvantaged regions, europe must show how dynamic it can be and how dynamic it is. the community's financing policy must be guided by this spirit of economic dynamism. i would like to say this very specifically. i also regret, mr president, that after yesterday's votes, which were as important as those on the environmental life cycle, tyres, marmalades and cream of brown - all equally important votes - we are obliged to discuss employment policy now, in the absence of the council. i regret the conditions under which we had to draw up this report, given the ambiguity surrounding it. you are indeed making a report on the guidelines, a legislative report, but you cannot amend it because the guidelines have been fixed for three years, as if the environmental context, the international, sociological, financial and fiscal context were not changing in this matter.

in writing. - (fr) the the idea behind the radical reform of the railways is commendable. in fact, the original aim was to restore the balance between rail and road and to promote the choice of environmentally friendly modes of transport. however, under the guise of attractiveness, we have embarked on an extreme and poorly controlled liberalisation. we must not be fooled, the real purpose of liberalization is to allow a few large private groups to share some extremely lucrative markets among themselves. what happens to life in the most backward and least profitable geographical areas, which are of little interest to private operators in their quest for profit? let us not forget the special status of rail transport, particularly in france, where it contributes to the social cohesion and harmonious development of the country as a public service. moreover, liberalisation seems to be incompatible with security, as some have had to renationalize as a result of repeated accidents. finally, as the rapporteur, mr jarzembowski, has acknowledged, the opening up of the rail freight market will lead to increased competition, which may reduce the number of jobs. all these are reasons why the members of hunting, fisheries, nature and tradition will vote against a common railway market based on social dumping and without a prior examination of the implications for those who are most affected by it, namely users and employees.

- the next item is the statement by the commission on the european economic and social model.
the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am pleased that at this unique historic moment for the european union i have the opportunity to discuss with you, the representatives of 450 million people and a union of markets, economies, peoples and societies, the two fundamental foundations on which the european union is based: the economic and social model. the european economic model is about the integration of markets and economies and the coordination of economic policies. the european social model is based on ensuring a high level of social protection, education and social dialogue, based on good economic performance. these two models are two sides of the same coin. they represent the two characteristics which distinguish the european union from other regions of the world. moreover, they have contributed not only to decades of growing prosperity for all citizens but also to the consolidation of peace and friendship among the peoples of europe. as regards the european economic model, the treaty provides for the implementation of an economic policy based on close coordination of the economic policies of the member states. highly integrated and interdependent economies sharing a common market and a common currency need effective economic policy coordination to benefit from it. to this end, a detailed economic policy framework has been established in the european union. in this context, the expression 'economic policy coordination' is used as a general term covering a whole range of interactions between policy-makers, both at national and european union level. methods used include exchanging information, discussing best practice, engaging in policy dialogue, developing commonly agreed policy rules and objectives, and undertaking jointly defined actions. the uniqueness of the coordination framework in economic and monetary union lies in the fact that an independent supranational european central bank has been entrusted with the conduct of a single monetary policy, while responsibility for economic, fiscal and structural policies remains decentralised in the hands of national authorities, but subject to common rules. the european central bank formulates monetary policy in the light of developments in the euro area as a whole and is therefore in a position to respond in the best possible way to any major crises that may affect the single currency area. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. many of the components of the economic coordination framework are closely linked to the overall lisbon strategy, a strategy of structural reforms with economic, social and environmental dimensions. the economic policy framework gives each country's national policy a considerable degree of autonomy in important areas and reflects the application of the principle of subsidiarity, which is based on a strong economic and political logic. in certain specific areas, such as the single market, competition policy and budget deficits, common rules need to be applied and reliable measures to ensure that they are respected. in other areas, such as the level and composition of public expenditure, structural policies and social welfare benefits, there are no strong arguments for transferring policy-making to a supranational level. decentralisation of policy-making gives national authorities the necessary room for manoeuvre to implement policies in line with national economic structures and preferences and to adapt to economic developments in each country. it also provides the possibility of ensuring the beneficial effects of competition policy. macroeconomic coordination in the euro area is generally based on dialogue and consensus. it aims at maintaining a sound and stable macroeconomic framework and at optimising the policy mix in the short term to address cyclical developments. its main objective is to ensure that economic growth does not fall short of its real potential. the effects of structural policies in partner countries and the shared benefits of economic and monetary union may not be as readily perceived as the consequences of macroeconomic policies. however, it is clear that the existence of efficient and flexible markets is crucial to increasing growth potential and ensuring the smooth functioning of economic and monetary union. in order to avoid distortions and ensure the proper functioning of the internal market, structural policies which have a direct impact on the functioning of the internal market and competition are subject to stronger forms of coordination. now, what is the european social model? the barcelona european council conclusions describe it as a model based on good economic performance, a high level of social protection and education and social dialogue. the european social model thus supports the parallel development of economic and social prosperity and is based on the interdependence between economic efficiency and social progress. despite the differences between our national systems, there is indeed this particular european social model, which is being strengthened by european social policies aimed at consolidating europe's economic strength. the european social model, in its various forms in the union, has played a key role in contributing to the continuous increase in productivity and the continuous improvement of the social level throughout the union, while ensuring that the benefits are spread as widely as possible. however, to improve its efficiency, this model needs to be modernised. the social partners have a very important role to play in this respect. reform is also facilitated by cooperation at european level, which is currently the case with issues such as employment, social inclusion and pension reform. the social policy agenda plays a crucial role in modernising the european social model. it is guided by the lisbon strategic objective, according to which europe must strive to become a more competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy, capable of ensuring sustainable economic growth, with more and better jobs and greater social cohesion. this clearly reflects the perception that the lisbon objective was a single strategic objective and not three competing pursuits. it is clear that securing more and better jobs or promoting social cohesion are elements that can support competitiveness and improve economic performance. the competitiveness ranking of the world economic forum, in which european countries such as finland, sweden and denmark are clearly in the lead, clearly underlines the crucial importance of this interaction. the success of the social policy agenda depends on many factors and this is a major advantage, as it broadens the range of actors involved in the implementation of the agenda and thereby strengthens the commitment to modernise the european social model. the social partners have a crucial role to play in this respect. social policies are therefore not simply the result of good economic performance but are also a factor with a substantial contribution to economic growth. the modernisation of the social model means mr president, mr minister, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the french delegation of our group considers the stability and growth pact to be one of the pillars of the european economy and the european currency. we want it to be able to be applied effectively in order to control public expenditure, to combat excessive deficits and to ensure the sound management of the public finances of the member states. that is why we support the commission's proposal and welcome the positive response of the council of ministers. the commission's proposal, drawing on the lessons of experience, is nothing more nor less than to make the rules of the pact fully and intelligently applicable without changing the two main criteria: the percentage of the deficit and the percentage of the debt. the communication of 3 september is based on principles which we approve of: allowing the commission to issue early warnings, focusing on the level of debt, building up budget surpluses in a high-conjunction environment to allow itself room for manoeuvre to deal with the slowdown in activity - this is the squirrel strategy - taking account of exceptional circumstances, a notion which the council of ministers must rigorously frame and, finally, coordinating the major economic policy objectives with the decisions of national parliaments. the proposal thus attaches greater importance to economic developments and seeks to avoid the risks that dogmatism may pose to activity and employment. for example, if france can make a strong contribution to growth in europe this year, it is probably because the pact has not been applied to it as a matter of course. we also welcome the appointment of a permanent president of the eurogroup, jean-claude juncker. all of this is in the right direction. in future, fiscal policy will contribute more to growth and thus play a decisive role in achieving the lisbon objectives, which set the horizon for the european union's competitiveness and prosperity.

mr president, when we know that the 'no' of one country can upset the adoption of the constitutional treaty for the whole of the european union, we can no longer consider that the ratification procedures are national. it is well known that the ratification of treaties, and particularly of referendums, is marred by internal political issues. france has recently given a pitiful example. it is therefore necessary, as far as possible, to denationalize the debate and to get the heads of state to coordinate their action with a view to successive ratifications; in order to create a positive adoption spiral, it will be necessary to avoid that the most reluctant countries speak first. in this sense, the proposal to have all the countries of the union vote during the same period, namely from 5 to 8 may 2005, should make it possible to put the strength of the symbols at the service of adoption. the symbol of unity of place: a european union which would speak in its entirety at the same time, as opposed to 25 countries voting one after the other; the symbol of the unity of a text: common question, common answer; the symbol of the unit of time: the whole of the union voting at the same time, while respecting the national traditions of elections held during the week or on sundays, from thursday 5 to sunday 8; and finally, the symbol of may 8, 2005, the 60th anniversary of the last conflict that pitted us all against each other. it is therefore on the basis of these 60 years of peace, thanks to the european union, that we could build the europe of tomorrow. that's the whole point of this proposal.
