mr president, mr president of the commission, to assess in three minutes the work done by the commission over five years is to square the circle. i shall therefore limit myself to pointing out a few points of reference which, in our view, illustrate the important trends which have marked and are still marking the action of the executive of the union and the union in general. i'm not questioning people. i'm challenging a policy. the current commission has brilliant personalities, from pascal lamy to chris patten, who have transcended political and national divisions. the problem is the orientation. the first example is the lisbon agenda. four years after the adoption of what the european council called a new strategic objective for the decade, where are we? one of the stated ambitions was, i recall, to achieve full employment. the commission's own figures now show that for the first time in ten years we are destroying more jobs than we are creating. the other ambition was to build the most dynamic knowledge economy in the world. the commission acknowledges a general decline in investment in key areas such as research, education and training. one figure quoted by the commission is even frightening: more than 17% of young europeans aged 15 do not have the minimum skills required: reading, writing, arithmetic. it was therefore to be expected that at least some questioning would begin, a hint of doubt about the relevance of the liberal leap forward of recent years, for which these failures could be the ransom. well, no, the question is never asked. during the crisis, the liberal wave continues and expands. secondly, the tempere programme of 1999, in particular the european policy on asylum and migration. has what human rights activists called fortress europe led to satisfactory results in controlling the so-called migratory flows? no, as evidenced by the repeated tragedies off the coast of sicily. so, are we resolved to tackle the problems from the other end, that is, to shift the ruthless rules of the global economy in an attempt to stop these survival migrations at their source? no, you can't! the commission is launching pilot projects to set up detention centres for refugees intercepted at sea on the southern shore of the mediterranean, without fearing ethical, humanitarian and legal problems. what's the next step? the transatlantic relationship is a final example. in the aftermath of 9/11, the idea had been floating around that our expression of solidarity with the american people was not tantamount to a docile acceptance of the views of its leaders on international security. allies but not aligned, they used to say. this did not prevent the commission from telling president bush at the transatlantic summit in june 2003, that is to say after the start of the war in iraq, that, and i quote, 'when europe and the united states are united, no enemy can stand against us'. history has not really validated this bold shortcut since then... but what public lesson has been learned? that is where the problem lies, mr president. there is never a confrontation of options: business as usual. it is time to instill a critical spirit in our institutions: contradiction is the engine of progress. the rapporteur. mr president, mr president of the central bank, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to commend the quality and the innovative nature of the european central bank's 2003 report, which was presented under the responsibility of mr trichet. the analysis of a period like 2003 has two aspects: what really happened in 2003 and what was decided in 2003? these are two different things, since monetary decisions have a delayed effect on real developments, of the order of 12 to 18 months according to econometrics. so it is a question of discussing the policy of 2002 and its changes in 2003. so, first of all, 2003 is a great price stability: a little over 2% at the beginning of the year and rather a little less at the end of the year, despite the rise in oil prices. the european union is unfortunately also stagnating quite impressively compared with its major competitors, be they the united states, japan, china, etc. it is therefore with this in mind that we must analyse the changes, both practical and doctrinal, made by the european central bank in 2003. let us start with the practical changes: while throughout 2002 the central bank had maintained its interest rates, practically until december, in contrast to the policy of our neighbours, the bank of england itself and the us federal reserve, which had reduced their interest rates very rapidly. on the contrary, from december 2002 and throughout, say, the first half of 2003, there was a very rapid fall in interest rates in europe, which actually began to have a positive effect in 2004. this fall in interest rates is illustrated by what has been called the "may 8th statement", which is dissected, dissected, explained in a prodigiously interesting way in the ecb's 2003 report, and we must fully subscribe to this inflation and its justification in the 2003 report. firstly, to deal with a risk of deflation, we are told, it is important that there is inflation below, but close to 2%, so that real interest rates can be brought down to a possible negative level. secondly, we are told that m3 is important in the long run, but not in the setting of monetary policy, and i believe that both these theses are indeed fully justified. our report approves this major change, and we will table amendments to make it even clearer. for the future, the 2003 report also contains an extremely important point, namely a clear statement by the european central bank, as a public authority, to say that it is responsible to the citizens and that its responsibility passes through dialogue with the european parliament. i believe that by positioning itself as a kind of executive branch, since it recognises that its relationship with the citizens is mediated by parliament, this report by the european central bank is taking a big step forward. i believe that this dialogue will have to be deepened in the future and we are making proposals in this respect in our report. thirdly, in our proposals for the future, we are obviously thinking of the entry of new countries. we ask that these countries be treated on an equal footing and with the same criteria for the interpretation of the convergence criteria as those applied to all countries up to now. there are no two weights, two measures: the same rules apply for 1997 and 2005, 2006, 2007. finally, we must start thinking about the new generation of banknotes. we consider that the one and two cent coins should be retained. many of us think that a one-euro note should be introduced. finally, we insist that banknotes should bring citizens closer to their currency. it's time to put living things on our currency, as every country in the world does.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, apart from the uncertainty surrounding the oil price, the central bank has done a fairly good job of keeping prices stable. is the euro area economy doing well? mr president, commissioner, in the last few months the steady rise in the price of a barrel has aggravated the crisis in the european fisheries sector. it directly affects the pay of the crews, but also the balance of the profit and loss account of the companies, which, as you have said, can hardly, if at all, pass on the effects of the sale of fish prices, given the specific nature of this type of market. the previous crisis, ten years ago, had already had a cascading effect, weakening the management and financing structures of the sector and thus seriously compromising the economy of the regions concerned. we are facing a similar situation of economic and social distress today, which the governments of the member states are trying, or will try, to deal with by providing, as you said, responses in accordance with community rules. however, these measures can only be conservative and cannot claim to respond effectively and sustainably to a situation of high fuel prices. the community's discourse, which is almost exclusively oriented towards, i quote, 'the sustainable management of fisheries resources in order to safeguard the interests of future generations', is no longer credible as it stands, since it risks leading to a situation in which the european union would no longer be able to exploit this resource for lack of professionals to take charge of it. how can we, in these circumstances, contribute to the real objective of our common fisheries policy, which is for me to contribute, together with the common agricultural policy, to the preservation of the capacity of our continent to provide food? the commissioner, my question will be the one i prepared with my colleagues from the committee on fisheries: does the commission undertake to intervene in favour of the areas most seriously affected? does it intend, for example, to make proposals to enable the existing instrument, the financial instrument for fisheries guidance, or the future european fisheries fund, or any other mechanism, to intervene in conjunction with the community and thus safeguard the future of regions which have no real alternative?
mr president, the increase in fuel prices is of course affecting many sectors of the european economy, particularly those linked to transport. but the most acute problems are clearly in the primary production sectors: agriculture and fisheries. it is clear that our debate is not entirely satisfactory because, if we want to kiss too much, we embrace badly enough: we should concentrate on these two subjects. the most serious difficulties are in the fisheries sector for one or two very simple reasons. in just over a year the price of diesel fuel for fishermen has doubled and to catch one kilo of fish, it takes about one litre of fuel. that is why i was literally astonished, as were my colleagues, and appalled by the statements of the commissioner responsible for fisheries, who said that the problem could be solved simply by passing the amount of the increase in fuel on to the fish price. that's naturally impossible. this is the very type of false reasoning that will turn consumers away from the very product that you want to promote: fish. i believe that the memory of the very disruptive crisis of 1993-94 shows us that very rapid action would be necessary. the proposals made earlier, in particular by mrs fraga and the chairman of our committee on fisheries, general morillon, were: capping the cost of diesel, reducing the financial, social and fiscal burdens, and also, most certainly, making progress adapted to the needs of fishermen in very serious difficulties, since there are already many of them. we therefore expect the commission to adopt a position which is both understandable and appropriate to avoid the disruption of areas heavily dependent on fishing. in other words, both european measures for crisis periods and national measures adapted to local situations would be needed.
the commission mr president, i wanted to make a few comments on the speeches that have been made in the debate, many of whose arguments and statements i fully agree with. firstly, in relation to the estimates of what is happening and what will happen with the evolution of oil prices and the impact that this has on the european economy in general. i think it is important to stress once again that we must be realistic in assessing the impact, and in this crisis, in this rise in the price of oil, which is very important in dollars, the impact on european economies is being much smaller than in previous crises. the impact on the economy as a whole should therefore not be exaggerated, regardless of the particularly sensitive and socially painful consequences in some specific sectors. secondly, i think we should be cautious in assessing the evolution that the price of oil may follow, in anticipating judgments about what that evolution may be. it is true that there are some economists who are talking about 60 and 70 dollars, but it is also true that the futures markets are trading downwards from the current level of 50 dollars a barrel and that, therefore, market operators are anticipating not further increases in the price of oil but rather a trend over the next two years towards a moderation of the market situation insofar as, as some of you have said, part of the increase in the price of oil that has occurred in recent months does not respond either to the objective situation of supply and demand in the market or even to the rest of the geopolitical factors that are affecting the situation, but to speculative operations that cannot be maintained over a long period of time in a permanent way. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. thirdly, i agree completely and completely with all those of you who have insisted on the need to continue to look at the need for energy efficiency and policies to reduce our dependence on oil as an energy source. i believe that the european union has made important progress in this area over the last 20 or 25 years and that we must continue to deepen this progress and intensify, as far as necessary - and i believe that in some respects it is clearly necessary - common action at european level in energy policy. for example, if i were to tell you that if the price of oil were to remain at $50 a barrel for the next two years, until the end of 2006, this would have an impact on the european union economy around a point of reducing growth, in the united states economy the impact would be much higher, because its degree of energy dependence on oil as a primary source of energy is much higher than that of the countries of the european union. and of course, in so far as the impact of the price of oil is negative, but not equally distributed among the different sectors of our society and the different productive sectors, it is clear that there is a need, as many of you have pointed out, to redistribute efforts according to the situation of the sectors most affected by the rise. and most of those who have referred to this unequal burden of effort have alluded, quite rightly, to the fisheries sector first and foremost, and also to the agricultural sector. what are the rules and the framework for dealing with this distribution of effort or this particularly intense compensation in the sectors most affected by the rise in oil prices? i repeat three criteria. first of all, obviously, attention must be paid to the principle of coordination - it is not good for anyone that unilateral measures are taken at national level on matters which must be decided at european level, whether by the ecofin council or by the agriculture council. the agriculture council began to discuss this question on 18 december and in the first debate the positions of the various member states were not unanimous. so it is true that the commission has to take initiatives and the new commission - which i hope will be confirmed next wednesday - will, as you know, not only have a new commissioner for agriculture - new in this case - but also a commissioner specifically dedicated to fisheries, mr borg, and a new commissioner for energy, as the honourable member said. but in addition to the commission's initiatives, consensus must be reached at council level both at the level of coordination, which is the responsibility of the ecofin council, as regards fiscal measures, and as regards measures which, where appropriate, could be taken at the level of the productive sectors, to which reference was made in the first debate on 18 december. there was no complete agreement between the member states. finally, we are all aware that we will have to continue discussing this issue in the coming months, but i repeat what i said at the beginning, we must do so with the awareness that, structurally, the oil market will never be the same as it was ten, twenty or twenty-five years ago, not least because there are new energy-consuming countries with extraordinary economic power and a very strong level of growth, but the lines along which european energy policy has been running are sound lines that must not be corrected in their direction but intensified in their power.

export policy in the medium term, the diversification and reorientation of the production of arms companies towards other products to avoid social disasters and the loss of skills, the creation of a european agency for the control of arms exports and, above all, the creation of a tax on arms exports for the benefit of the victims of conflicts and the fight against poverty. if the union were to adopt these proposals and translate them into specific legal measures, this would be a considerable step forward and would create a dynamic for putting pressure on countries such as the united states, china, ukraine, russia and israel. if all this could be combined, to make it even more effective, with measures to control the origin of capital in tax havens established in the territory of the union, then we would have taken a step towards safeguarding humanity. in conclusion, may i quote albert einstein: "either mankind will destroy the weapons, or the weapons will destroy mankind".

mr president, with climate change, humanity is faced with a challenge to civilization, since it is a question of the preservation of species and the great natural balances. this calls for a renewed vision of our concepts of progress and development. this problem will increasingly dominate the common existence of men during this century. the increase in extreme weather events confirms that the effects of global warming are already being felt. profound changes are now inevitable. the european union seems determined to achieve the objectives of the kyoto protocol, but much remains to be done to prepare people for the changes that are coming. the definition and implementation of a genuine adaptation policy is urgent, it is unavoidable. we must draw the political consequences from the work of scientists and, in particular, from the report of the european environment agency, which details the multiple impacts of global warming in europe, which, it should be remembered, is certainly the smallest of the world's continents, but also the one with the largest number of sea facades. at the initiative of the french national observatory on the effects of climate change, which i chair, the 155 maritime peripheral regions of europe and the mediterranean have already decided to meet in 2005 in marseille to discuss the issue of adaptation. we count on the support of the commission in this process, which can contribute to the development of a genuine european strategy for adaptation to the current climate change. this has become an essential part of the community's climate change action programme and now needs to be extended.
the council received mr kok's report on the revision of the lisbon strategy. the results are far below the targets set in 2000. too many priorities drowned out the priorities. what was under the community method liberalisation has advanced, what required the commitment of the states and what was under the open method of coordination investment in research, innovation, training, the quality of social dialogue, human capital has not followed. national appropriation has not taken place either: much remains to be done in this area. we welcome the reaffirmation of the need to maintain the balance between the three dimensions of the lisbon strategy: economic, social and environmental. we are convinced that more growth and competitiveness of the european economy is essential to the preservation of the european social and environmental model. but we still have to debate the link between these dimensions and the conditions for sustainable growth in europe. we are facing a temptation, which seems to us to be that of ease, to rely more and more on liberalization: liberalization of services, of the labour market, of social systems. but if we continue down this slope, there will soon be little left of the european model, its specificity, its strengths, its assets, which do not lie in the downward alignment towards the social level of some of our new international competitors (i am thinking of china and india), but in the competition for excellence, for quality, for the high end, for innovation. we are therefore convinced that investment in human capital, in a high level of lifelong training for workers, in the quality of public services and in european environmental standards, in good social dialogue, are all productive factors, factors of competitiveness and also conditions for the acceptance of reforms when they are needed. this is why these are not just costs, burdens or rigidities, but points of support for the success of a new strategy for development and growth in the european union. we want growth and jobs to be the priority, and i believe that this will also require a better coordination of all the instruments of european policies, mr president, i would like to return to the hague programme and ask the council a few questions on this subject. there is no doubt that there is a major innovation in the move to qualified majority voting for title iv. there are the comments made by colleagues on the reservations about legal immigration, but i would like to ask more specifically about the extreme importance of the external dimension of asylum and immigration policies. the european union's ability to conclude partnership and cooperation agreements for return, readmission, capacity building, border control, police and judicial cooperation, in other words a set of agreements with third countries, which are not subject to co-decision, is increasingly seen as a basis for these agreements. we are concerned on two counts, because we have no confidence in people like schily or pisanu who have put forward ideas such as camps, immigration portals or counters outside the union. even though these words have been largely rejected, even though they are not included in the hague programme, even though they have been rejected en masse by hundreds of ngos and many members of parliament, including europeans, we are concerned because in this hague draft there is a reference to a feasibility study on the processing of asylum applications outside the union and we also know that a budget of one million euros has been released to enable unhcr to develop asylum capacity in north african countries. we therefore wonder whether this does not constitute both a democratic divestiture of the european parliament and a transfer of responsibilities of the european parliament and the european union in the field of asylum and immigration, responsibilities which would be shifted to third countries, whose capacities in this area are much less than ours.
mr president, on 4 and 5 november the council adopted, with the hague programme, the new priorities for europe with a view to strengthening the area of security, freedom and justice. we are pleased to see that the council has heard the requests of the european parliament, in particular on the transition to codecision and qualified majority voting, for example in the field of asylum, immigration and the fight against terrorism, without forgetting the civil aspect of justice. we regret, however, that in this programme the council seems again to be limiting itself to a declaration of good intentions. while welcoming the progress made over the past five years, particularly with regard to the foundations of a common asylum and immigration policy, the harmonisation of border controls and the improvement of judicial cooperation, it would be appropriate to point out the obstacles that some member states are putting in the way of progress in the area of justice. it would also be fair to recall that the harmonization of asylum has been minimal. the council regrets that not all the objectives have been met, but it does not see any concrete measures to prevent this from happening again in the years to come. finally, we are particularly concerned about the parallel between the fight against terrorism, organised crime and illegal immigration. this parallel implies that illegal immigrants are seen as potential criminals or terrorists, which is completely unacceptable. these people are forced to leave their home countries because of untenable living conditions or because of persecution. while a comprehensive approach to asylum, immigration and external border control policies is necessary, it must not, however, be at the expense of the fundamental rights of migrants.

in writing. for 30 years, a third of the island of cyprus has been occupied by the turkish army, which has ethnically cleansed the orthodox cypriots from their lands and given them to turkish settlers from anatolia. the european institutions not only do not condemn this violation of international law, which affects a member state, but now finance it. why would you do that ? because our leaders want to remove all obstacles to the entry of turkey, an asian and muslim country, into europe. after having flouted the basic rules of geography, which say that turkey is not a european state, they are now flouting the principles of international law, which they also insist on using to teach lessons to the whole world. the only recourse left to the european nations is to reject next year the constitution of this europe from brussels.
in writing. we are certainly the only ones here who do not agree with the conclusions of the brussels summit. we cannot fully endorse the lisbon strategy. behind the laudable aims stated - such as employment, training, economic growth - and the means allegedly used - coordination - this strategy is a real instrument for further harmonization of national economic and social policies. it is in the direction of dismantling public services and the regression of our social protection systems. we are absolutely opposed to the accelerated communitization of immigration policies, which are only intended to organise migration flows, to replace ageing european populations. it provides for even fewer internal controls without guaranteeing a strengthening of europe's external borders. giving the commission the right of initiative and the european parliament the right of codecision in these matters, depriving the national parliaments of any power, even of control, and the states of their right of veto, is a guarantee that lax proposals will be made even more lax by this assembly. that is why we shall vote against all the resolutions before us today.

taxation systems for savings income, some residents of the member states were able to escape, in their state of residence, any form of taxation on interest received in another state. the commission has therefore drawn up a draft directive to remedy a situation which favours the development of harmful competition in taxation, since capital flows tend to flow to non-eu countries with abnormally low taxation. the lack of information on such revenues thus hinders the proper functioning of the single market. in this context, the council authorised the commission, by its decision of 16 october 2001, to negotiate appropriate agreements with switzerland, the united states of america, andorra, lichtenstein, monaco and san marino with a view to ensuring that these countries adopt measures equivalent to those applied within the union, in order to guarantee effective taxation of savings income in the form of interest payments. since then, on 3 june 2003, the council adopted the directive on taxation of savings income in the form of interest payments, which provides in particular for a system for the exchange of information. three member states, austria, belgium and luxembourg, have imposed conditions on the lifting of banking secrecy. they have obtained a transitional period during which they are allowed to levy a tax instead of this exchange of information. in the meantime, agreements have been negotiated with switzerland, andorra, lichtenstein, san marino and monaco. as regards the united states of america, the current framework of bilateral relations between the member states and the united states in tax matters has made it possible to assess that equivalent measures already exist. the agreements between the european community and switzerland, andorra and lichtenstein were submitted to parliament very recently and were adopted. the two last agreements to be submitted to parliament are the agreement with monaco and the one with san marino. the components of these two agreements are similar to those of the agreements examined above. i would like to recall briefly: the use of the source shared with the state of residence, the voluntary transmission of information at the initiative of the recipient of income, the review clause, the commitment to make progress in the exchange of information in the event of tax fraud. these two agreements, like the previous ones, mark an important step forward on the political front. the agreements will ensure that the countries concerned adopt measures equivalent to those which must be applied within the european union for the effective taxation of savings income in the form of interest payments made in one state and intended for beneficiaries resident in another state. this mechanism is likely to allow effective taxation, which is necessary to combat harmful tax competition and to contribute to improving the functioning of the single market. to achieve this objective, the automatic exchange of information between tax administrations provided for in directive 2003/48/ec is an appropriate means. with these two agreements, the necessary phase of the conclusion of agreements prior to the application of the directive for the states i mentioned earlier is completed. the implementation of these agreements was originally scheduled for 1 january 2005, but was postponed to 1 july 2005 by council decision of 19 july 2004. the various conditions for implementation should be or will be fulfilled by that date. it is important that this date be respected so that the whole system can be applied under good conditions.

mr president, next friday the european council in brussels will take a decision which will affect the future of the european union: the decision to open accession negotiations with turkey. however, each time accession negotiations have been opened, they have ended in accession. i therefore strongly urge you, ladies and gentlemen, to take account of the amendment we tabled, which calls for the establishment of a privileged partnership with turkey. as i said in this house in november 2002, turkey has no intention of joining the european union. firstly, the treaties state that the european union is open to european countries; however, 95% of turkey's territory, including its capital ankara, is in asia. secondly, the more we enlarge the union, the more we dilute it, the further we move away from political europe and the less able we will be to pursue common policies together. thirdly, if turkey were to join the union, it would be the most populous country by 2015, with 80 million inhabitants, which would mean that it would have the largest number of meps in this parliament and a preponderant weight in the european council. finally, if we accept turkey into the union, what argument will we put forward tomorrow against all the other candidates for membership who will be knocking on our door: ukraine, morocco, algeria, etc? all these reasons, not to mention the non-compliance with the copenhagen criteria, the non-recognition of the armenian genocide or the non-recognition of a country of the european union, are in favour of a decision on friday that goes beyond the debate on accession or exclusion. and that is the solution, i repeat, of the privileged partnership. it should be clear that this is not an anti-turkish position but a pro-european one.

commission. mr president, i thank you and the honourable members for a very rich, analytical and multi-dimensional debate, which has covered virtually the whole spectrum of european public opinion ranging from future peace dividends to past crusades and, more seriously, from women's rights to religious communities and their rights in turkey. i will touch on a limited number of questions that members addressed directly to the commission. first, there have been numerous requests for rigorous monitoring of legal reforms and human rights in general. i fully agree with this. the rigorous monitoring mechanism and the annexed suspension clause are indeed at the core of our negotiation strategy with regard to turkey in the coming years. it is also very much in the interests of turkey because it maintains the strong incentive to implement and consolidate the necessary legal and political reforms. we will be preparing a monitoring report during 2005 concerning the fulfilment of criteria in the field of human rights in general. these criteria include the issue of trade union rights, which mr rasmussen raised. he referred to an ongoing court case of which the commission is aware. we are monitoring this case very closely. in our report we consider this to be a serious test case with regard to the depth of legal reform in turkey, which touches upon trade union rights, language rights and the rights of minorities in turkey. this also involves the question of non-muslim religious minorities, which has been addressed in depth by mr eurlings in his report and referred to by several members here this evening. i would like to underline that although freedom of religion is guaranteed by the turkish constitution, non-muslim religious communities nevertheless face a series of structural difficulties, such as the lack of a legal personality and the lack of full economic rights. the turkish authorities are committed to adopting a law addressing these structural problems. a draft law on foundations is currently being discussed and the commission has been officially invited to submit its comments to the turkish authorities on this critical piece of legislation. we will continue to have dialogue and put pressure on the turkish government on this particular subject. concerning the enforcement mechanism of the suspension clause, to which mr duff referred, the origin of the suspension clause lies in the development of the acquis communautaire. the union now has clauses in article 7 of the treaty on european union and in the draft constitutional treaty that provide for a procedure to deal with cases where a member state seriously and persistently breaches the basic principles of the union. it is only logical and normal that similar rules should also apply to candidate countries. in fact, it has always been the case even in the past that such serious situations would lead to a suspension of negotiations. thus the inclusion of an explicit suspension procedure is based on a new acquis and the commission will base its proposal on these principles of the treaty. thus i am fully in agreement with mr nicolaï and with mr duff. on the question of the privileged partnership, the instrument of a special partnership is provided for under the draft constitutional treaty. it is intended to give special treatment to neighbours or other partners representing a strategic interest for the european union. the idea of the special partnership underlines in particular the new neighbourhood policy, which the eu seeks to extend to its eastern and southern neighbours. this initiative does not apply to turkey, which has been a candidate country since the helsinki summit in 1999. it is hard to figure out how any more could be offered to turkey than it already has under the privileged partnership. first of all, turkey and the eu are bound by a customs union which constitutes a far-reaching instrument of bilateral cooperation in the area of trade and economic cooperation, implying a great degree of economic integration. second, turkey already participates in numerous community programmes in a wide range of areas such as culture, drugs, justice and home affairs, education, research and development. third, in the key area of security and defence, turkey participates as a nato member – via both nato and the european security and defence policy – in the development of eu security operations. for instance, there are turkish troops in many countries in the balkans, and even in the 'european army', as one british newspaper recently dubbed the 'althea' operation in bosnia. with regard to the privileged partnership, and as mr nicolaï also said, in my view the clear objective of the accession negotiations will and should be accession if turkey meets all the criteria for membership by the end of the negotiations. it would not be wise to set any final target date because we have recently learned that schedule should not override substance. we should set realistic targets, not deadlines that we cannot meet. finally, mr howitt asked about the start-date from the point of view of the commission. our mandate is to evaluate whether turkey fulfils the copenhagen political criteria. this is what we did. concerning the start-date of the negotiations, we trust the wisdom of the european council, of the prime ministers and presidents to make the political judgement with regard to when in 2005 they deem it appropriate to start the accession negotiations. from the point of view of the commission, i can say that we are ready to start work – in the words of parliament's resolution – 'without undue delay'. i only hope that somebody will explain to me the difference between 'undue' and 'due' delay. nevertheless, we are ready to work without delay once the negotiations have been made and the process can be started. mr swoboda, mr szent-iványi and several others made the very important point that if we succeed in this long process of negotiations, it should and will make the eu strategically stronger. this is the fundamental issue at stake here and the strategic, geopolitical and geocultural crux of the matter. we can learn some lessons from history – we do not have to apply them blindly, but we can indeed learn something. during the cold war, europe contained communism and the soviet union and cooperated in terms of enhancing security and human rights with impressive results. we can see this from the significant number of colleagues from free eastern and central europe who are here among us today as members of this parliament. now and in the future, the challenge is very much the relationship between europe and islam. europe must, on the one hand, contain islamic fundamentalism using all the means available and, on the other hand, it must build bridges and dialogue with those representing moderate islam. if, after long and difficult negotiations, we achieve a situation where the rule of law genuinely prevails in turkey, and where european democracy meets a predominantly muslim population, then that would certainly be an asset for europe and a very important crossroads of civilisations.

the next item is the oral question to the commission by mr josep borrell fontelles, on behalf of the temporary committee on the political challenges and budgetary means of the enlarged union, on the preparation of the next financial framework.
commission. mr president, i am supposed to say that officially i am responding on behalf of the commission to four questions from parliament, but i received a lot more. i will try to answer them as well as giving the 'official' response. i must say at the outset that in the commission there are no internal discussions on ceilings other than the official proposal that was presented to you and to the council. despite media rumours, this is not a subject for discussion in the commission. now the 'official' response to the first question: does the new commission endorse the structure of the new financial perspective? yes, the enlarged european union faces new challenges and needs to meet new expectations. we need to update the structure of our financial perspectives to better reflect these new priorities. this entails a new classification of expenditure to give a new profile for the union's finances. this more limited number of expenditure headings reflects the union's main priorities, making them more visible to european citizens and rationalising expenditure accordingly. this commission endorses the same priorities, i.e. transforming the european union into a dynamic knowledge-based economy, pursuing greater cohesion in the context of the enlargement of the european union, preserving and managing the european union's natural resources – including agriculture, fisheries and the environment – and developing the area of freedom, security and justice and the role of the union as a global partner. the proposals before us reflect the needs of the union, firstly because these priorities identify and represent a common consensus about where europe must intensify its actions. secondly, the proposed structure also offers a real step towards simplification and rationalisation, which was welcomed by parliament in its resolution of 22 april. finally, the proposals have already allowed both the council and parliament to have substantial discussions and prepare the ground for an agreement next year. the second question: does the new commission endorse the duration of the financial programmes which will commit the next commission and the next european parliament? let me assure you that the commission is fully aware of parliament's position – which was also expressed in the resolution of 22 april – in which it calls for a financial framework to be established for a period of only five years. however, we looked into this question and concluded that for the next programming period, seven years would be the best solution because the ceiling for market-related expenditure and direct payments – in agriculture, for example – has already been fixed by the european council until 2013. a seven-year timetable also maximises the benefits of long-term planning, in particular in cohesion policies. the third question: does the new commission endorse all the proposals in what is known as the 'prodi package', or does it consider that it should be readjusted and, if so, on which issues? as i said earlier, we endorse all the proposals. the commission stands by the package proposed earlier this year. we do not call it by that name: it is the commission's proposal and we endorse that proposal, namely the proposed financial framework, complemented by a series of legislative and non-legislative proposals adopted between february and september 2004. they have been submitted to the council and to various committees of this parliament. the commission foresees the adoption of the remaining necessary proposals early next year. the political project which underpins the financial perspectives is based on a number of well-established priorities on which a consensus already exists between the european institutions on the number of commitments already made, for example on agriculture, enlargement, lisbon, etc. building on this, the commission is now also preparing its five-year strategic objectives, which will be presented to parliament by the end of january 2005. the commission believes that the proposals constitute a good basis for an agreement for the next financial perspective. to reach such an agreement the commission will be taking an active part in the discussions and negotiations that will take place with the european parliament and the council. in this context, the commission will take fully into account the key points of the discussion and will strive to reach a political agreement by the end of june 2005. the fourth question: is the commission ready to take account of other institutions' priorities? the answer is yes. the commission will of course take careful account of parliament's position in relation to the initiatives already proposed and in view of those that will arrive in 2005. the package is already based on a very broad consensus about where actions are required, in the light of european parliament resolutions, european council conclusions and, indeed, discussions within the commission. the forthcoming discussions on the commission's strategic objectives are directly linked to this, and the commission attaches considerable importance to the establishment of common priorities. the constitution will mean a codified multiannual financial framework, and i would like a common vision for the next programming period to be our first step on this path. i would like to make two brief points in finalising the official answer to the question tabled. first, i wish to remind you of what president barroso has said in this house: the european union needs to match its political ambition with its financial resources. increased spending has been proposed because, with enlargement and with a demand for action in new areas, it was inevitable. we cannot have a larger european union with less money. secondly, i underline the commission's strong commitment to the need to respect the target of a political agreement by june 2005 and the adoption of legislative proposals by the end of that year. the irish and netherlands presidencies have achieved considerable progress during their respective terms in the council. we all need to sustain the momentum and actively support the efforts of the luxembourg presidency to achieve political agreement by the end of its term. the commission wishes the presidency well in the task of achieving the goals which will be useful for all european citizens. in writing. in its recommendation of 6 october, the commission, which has produced a solid report, ruled out turkey's recognition of the armenian genocide of 1915. this event resulted in the death of over a million people, nearly two thirds of the country's largest minority. the intention, the mass and systematic destruction, of this crime constitutes the first of the genocides of the 20th century, a genocide of which the turkish state still today fights against any reference. today, the worst thing would be silence. and the commission's silence may give the impression that the memory of such a tragedy does not concern it, that this is a problem between turks and armenians only. and it bothers me. not because of a religious, historical or social issue, but because it is a political issue that affects democracy and human rights. this is a question which is at the very foundations of the european union, which was born after the second world war when france and germany affirmed their desire to establish peace in europe, assuming the most tragic hours of the continent (even if the extent of the extermination of the jews was not fully recognized until later). the armenian question is therefore a decisive issue for europe, which aspires to be a free, anti-totalitarian area in which a modern and secular citizenship can flourish. in writing. as chair of the european parliament's delegation for the south caucasus, i welcome the large majority vote on the eurlings report on the opening of accession negotiations with turkey, and recall the major importance for the peoples of europe and for the stability of an entire continent of opening the doors of the european union to this country. i regret that the european union did not, from the very beginning of the discussions on turkey's possible accession, take up the issue of lifting the blockade and opening the borders with its armenian neighbour and that turkey did not take this historic opportunity to show its goodwill by opening its border with armenia. i reject, however, the use, particularly by the french right-wing political parties, of the armenian genocide and the question of borders to deny this opening to turkey. to make this argument on the eve of the council's decision to open negotiations is indecent and is only intended to hide the real reasons for turkey's refusal to join.
in writing. the european peoples, like the french, germans, greeks and austrians, are increasingly expressing their opposition to the entry into europe of turkey, an asian country belonging to the muslim world. the leaders of europe in brussels, especially mr chirac, know this. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the accession negotiations are concluded in good time. this statement, echoed in the camiel eurlings report, is untrue: since the first enlargement in 1972, all negotiations have been followed by the accession of the applicant country. the same will be true of turkey. especially since its islamist leaders have warned us that they will not make any concessions. if, on 17 december, the european council decides, against the wishes of the people, to open accession negotiations with the turkish government, the referendum on the european constitution will be the last chance for france to avoid its dissolution as a whole, with only its name european, in which turkey, the most populous state, will have a predominant role.
in writing. i am against any further enlargement until the union has deepened its political integration in order to become a powerful europe, a social europe. with each enlargement, the horizon of a federal europe was opened up. the entry of turkey will further dilute the european project. its integration into the current eu framework is not desirable. the question will be asked by all, and it is not linked to religion or geography: the european union must be a political project. this project is now problematic because it is reduced to a free trade area, which is less and less regulated. we must re-think the architecture of europe with a federal core, then a union of 27 countries and an area of enhanced cooperation with neighbouring countries such as turkey, but also other countries such as those in the maghreb, with which we have close links. the fact that we are now voting for the opening of negotiations takes this perspective away and continues the path of permanent enlargement. there are legitimate demands on turkey. but of course if that country does that, it will be impossible to refuse him entry. before any possible accession negotiations, the framework for the future of europe must be defined. we must reject enlargement and open up another cooperation with turkey.
in writing. i abstained in the final vote on the eurlings report. firstly, it would be reasonable not to consider any further enlargement without first settling the question of europe's frontiers. to push its limits indefinitely risks turning europe into a vast free trade area. the federalists cannot afford to make such a sacrifice. secondly, experience shows that the opening of negotiations inevitably leads to accession if the applicant country fulfils the required conditions, in particular the copenhagen criteria. although it is to be hoped that turkey will continue to make progress, particularly in the field of democracy and human rights, there is no guarantee that europe will be ready to provide itself with the means, particularly budgetary means, to carry out such an enlargement in a satisfactory manner for all. the vote on the abstention is therefore a warning signal to the european summit on 17 december: no further enlargement without further discussion! we must stop putting the peoples of europe in the face of the fait accompli by calling on them to ratify decisions taken without their consent many years ago by the heads of state or government.
in writing. this report is a further step towards the adoption of a single asylum procedure. curiously, it does not concern only political refugees, who should be the only ones entitled to claim asylum under the geneva convention. it also concerns all those who could benefit from 'subsidiary protection', i.e. those 'who cannot return home because of the general situation in their country of origin'. the future european asylum procedure will therefore concern all applicants for migration. it is true that in the europe without frontiers of brussels, the political tradition is to systematically encourage immigration. point 25 of the report states that 'a common asylum procedure at eu level based on high levels of settlement' is needed. in contrast, in this report on the rights of migrants, there is not a word about "illegal immigrants". the return policy is also strictly regulated: refusal of asylum must be duly justified in an 'authentic document' written in the language of the applicant, and charter flights are impossible. in addition, the possibility of setting up detention centres in transit countries is eliminated.
in writing. drug use is increasing throughout europe. the number of overdose deaths in the european union is around 7 000 a year, a figure that must be tripled for deaths indirectly linked to drugs (suicide, violence, aids, road accidents, etc.). brussels seems to want to tackle this scourge. the only thing it proposes in the fight against drugs is not to prevent young people from using drugs, nor to allow addicts to get away with it, but to 'sanitize' drug addiction. we are offered recovery facilities, controlled heroin injection rooms, needle exchange programs. we cannot accept such a policy. in the fight against drugs, prevention is essential, but so is repression. let us increase the penalties for drug dealers and introduce forensic medical monitoring for users. finally, let us not separate soft drugs from hard drugs. none of them are harmless. in fact, this simple classification has led to a considerable increase in cannabis use. it is worth noting that the links between the use of these drugs and mental health have been scientifically demonstrated (schizophrenia 30 to 50% higher among cannabis users).
in writing. the council will decide on the new eu drugs strategy 2005-2012 on 16 and 17 december. a political agreement has already been reached in the council in the absence of transparency and democratic control by parliament. the council has been very reluctant to respond to our repeated requests to transmit the state of its negotiations when we were discussing the same subject in the committee on civil liberties. i have today voted in favour of mr catania's report because the european parliament must show the council its vision of the new drugs strategy for the years to come. we see that the european strategy has had little success so far. at the same time, drug use has increased in europe. we therefore want to see more european coordination and cooperation so that europe can add value to the fight against the scourge of drugs while respecting the principle of subsidiarity. finally, we must give priority to the protection and health of drug users. we must therefore strengthen prevention, care and health policy to avoid human tragedy and reduce exclusion.
the rapporteur. mr president, i am presenting this report in a context which has been politically clarified in recent weeks. last week the commission was able to conclude the accession negotiations with romania on the last two chapters, the one on justice and home affairs and the one on competition. in addition, in recent weeks there have been parliamentary and then presidential elections which have led to a political alternation under conditions which have been recognized by all parties. this context does not, of course, lead me to change the philosophy and orientations of this report. i wanted to draw up and submit to the house a balanced report, that is to say a report which is both demanding and clear-sighted, because romania's situation raises many problems, but also a friendly report, because we have a common desire to bring romania and bulgaria into the union and because that country has worked to prepare its accession. this leads us to propose that we should both take note of the progress made by romania on the road to accession, but also be aware of the limits, the shortcomings and the extent of the road that still needs to be traveled, these two dimensions, the limits and the progress, being in fact present in all respects. the first concerns political criteria, and that is where the main difficulties lie. the limitations are there: reform of the civil service is insufficient, the use of emergency orders is undesirable and is completely excessive; the legislative process, as everyone knows, is imperfect. but beyond these limits, there are still a number of problems with freedom, and these are serious problems. i am thinking first of all of the freedom of information and expression, which is being curtailed for a large number of journalists. i am thinking of the judicial system, which is undoubtedly in need of improvement, although it is only just beginning to be improved. i am thinking of course of corruption, which remains endemic in romania, including at the highest level. on all these issues - freedom of expression, corruption, the judiciary and the police - i believe that the european parliament must be absolutely uncompromising. at the same time, we cannot ignore the undeniable progress. the commission recognised that romania met the copenhagen political criteria; the country has launched the reform of the public administration and the reform of the constitution has also been initiated. the judicial system, as i said, is beginning to improve and we are also seeing progress in child protection, which is what our own parliament wants, although we can go further. in sum, i believe that romania has listened to the recommendations of the commission and of our parliament, in particular those made at the instigation of the previous rapporteur, mrs nicholson. the same problem exists in terms of economic criteria: there are limits, macroeconomic stability is not yet guaranteed and poverty remains at an extremely high level. at the same time, we are making progress in the fight against social exclusion, in the fight against poverty and in the implementation of social protection legislation. finally, thirdly, everything that concerns the community acquis. on this point, as i said at the beginning, the negotiations are over. i do not think it is prudent to take them back, although i read that the president-elect intended to do so. i believe that the treaty must first be ratified and signed before it can be renegotiated. but we need to implement the legislation adopted, particularly on the free movement of goods and capital, financial control, the environment, industrial production, regional policy and justice and home affairs. this judgment, which i hope is balanced, justifies the conclusions i recommend, which are as follows: nothing prevents today the signing of a joint accession treaty - i insist - between romania and bulgaria, at the beginning of 2005, for accession in 2007. it is obviously a political decision, but it requires vigilance on the part of parliament and the commission through all the follow-up actions and other reports that we can present here. a final word on the amendments tabled. i think we did a good job in the committee on foreign affairs, which resulted in a very broad vote. there are two types of amendments to this report. there are those who bring substantial improvements, particularly on the question of social protection, human rights, the disabled, the protection of children and young people, recommendations on industrial policy and i am of course in favour of these. then there are other amendments which call into question the existence of a common accession treaty or which alter the nature and balance of the report, and i am obviously not in favour of them. we have taken a historic decision this morning to open negotiations with turkey. i think that concluding them with romania and bulgaria, and romania in particular, is a logical decision and it would be incomprehensible if we did not do both together.
on behalf of the group. mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, perhaps we should start with the question mr fava has rightly and appropriately asked, namely that of dialogue between our institutions. this is a recurring question, which is why we are here at this late hour and at this late time of the year. in this connection, we have heard from your lips, we have read - and you also said so at your hearing - that you wish to have a dialogue, which we can call as we wish, but which i understood to be regular, relevant, open, long-term, brief and structured. this is obviously a proposal, an offer of dialogue which parliament will take up because, as you know, members are very keen to have a thorough discussion both on the guidelines, on the continuous evaluation and on the information on the programming of this initiative. the ball is in our court, ladies and gentlemen, and i believe that the commission would be pleased to see a proposal from our ranks, our committees, our groups, in short, from this parliament, so that this dialogue can be set up very quickly - because we need it very urgently, with a group of colleagues who are fully motivated and competent on this issue, which is not lacking in this institution. let's go back to that initiative. i think it is worth repeating how much added value it brings to all the actions that the european union can develop in terms of democracy and human rights. perhaps it has not been sufficiently emphasized that this is the only means at our disposal for supporting, against the will of their governments, which are often autocratic or dictatorial, civil society, actors and ngos which develop actions under often extremely complicated conditions. it is the only instrument that enables us to do this and it is extremely valuable. i would also add that the aid thus given to these ngos is perceived on the ground as neutral, that is to say that there is no desire for domination or recovery in this subsidy action of the european union, and it is not perceived as such, contrary to what one can hear when american agencies are acting on the ground - at any rate one hears it very often in the maghreb. this is a very valuable asset, acquired by the quality of the european union's intervention. of course, there are limits to this quality. one of the limitations, and we all know many of them, is that ngos, for one reason or another, cannot be supported by this initiative. the governments of third countries which do not wish to see democratic movements developing within their borders do not lack resources and imagination. we have the case of legal ngos, supported by the initiative, to which subsidies are strictly prohibited by political decree, by direct censorship. so all the decisions have been made, but these ngos cannot benefit from the funds that have been allocated to them. we also have other examples of associations which simply do not have a legal existence. we must then find subterfuge, and so we need a capacity for flexibility and ingenuity on the ground to achieve our aims. i would like to conclude by saying that this debate would be useless if we did not have the prospects beyond 2007 in mind. and here, as other members have rightly done, i draw attention to the fact that we will have to work within this parliament to ensure that this precious asset, which can always be improved, can continue beyond 2006. this is the subject of the debates we are going to have to have at different levels in this parliament.
